To the Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester: To the Overseers of the Poor, ow, en of Property, and Ratepayers of the Townships of Antrobus, Fro&ham, Halton, Norley, Run- corn, and Seven Oaks, in the said County; To the Overseen of the Poor. Owners of Property, and Ratepayers of the Lordship of Frodsharn. in the said County; To the Guardians of the Poor of the Runcorn Union, in the said County; And to all others whom it may concern,

WHEREAS the Townships of Antrobus, Frodsham, Halton, Norley, Runcorn, and Seven Oaks, and the Lord- ship of Frodsham, in the Runcorn Union, in the County of Chester, are divided so that parts of the said Townships and Lordship are isolated and detached from the remainder, within the meaningof the Divided Parishes and Poor Law Amendment Act, 1878, and the Poor Law Act, 1879; and whereas it has been proposed, in pursuance of the said Acts, that each of the said isolated and detached parts be separated • from the said Townships and Lordship, and be amalgamated with some Parish or T wnship which it adjoins, or be otherwise dealt with under the said Acts; arid whereas it has been represented that parts of the Township of Frodsham and the Lordship of Prod- sham, although not isolated and detached from the remainder of the Township or Lordship, are so sit ua ,ed as to render the relief of the Poor in, or the local government of, such parts in conjunction with the residue of the Township or Lordship in- convenient. and that it is desirable that the said parts ot the said Township and Lordship should be separated therefrom and be amalgamated with the Township or Lordship in which the same may be locally included, or to which they may be annexed, so that the boundary be ween the said Township and Lordship sh, old "commence at the Helsby Boundary on the north side of the railway to smithy-lane, thence up Smithy-lane and the Church footpath to Pinmill-brow, thence up Howey- lane to Overton. thence along Towntield-lane, and down the Occupation-road numbered 307 in the Ordnance Survey, and in the line of fence between 312 and 313, thence along the fence between 312. and 315, and between 275 and 276, all in the Ordnance Survey, to tire river. All property lying to the south of the said boundary to be in the T ,wnship of Frodshatn Lord- ship, and all property lying to the north of the said boundary boun- daryaplotefrFedrodasshammay;";emernfurtwherb,ethadtestihreabinptou rbse. iabnne et eto hfTetorhwwe fe said Acts; and whereas it has also been repre- sented that parts of the Townships of Halton and Runcorn, Irheelierfemfatihnedeprooofr tihne, oaTownships,rltth:,eu gat ore isolatedesronsmi teunaatnt edo of, s :tut aocchttelpenaddreftr:tmil:,,e conjunction with the residue of the Townships inconvenient, and that it is desirable that the said parts of the said Townships should be separated therefrom, and be amalgamated with the Township in which the same ;may be locally included, or to which they may be annexed, so that the bounders between the said Townships , should "be from Halton Brook, along Astmore-lane to the bridge, thence following Smith's-lane and fences to the river; from Halton Brook down south side of Wood-lane to its junc- tion with Heath road, thence up the south side of Heath-road to the Weston Boundary, thence along the present boundary of Runcorn and Weston ;' or further, that the boundary be other- wise altered as may seem to be desirable id pursuance of the said Acts : and whereas the Local Government Board have appointed Illehard Ingram Dansey, Esquire, Barrister-at-Law, one of their Inspectors, to hold a Local inquiry in reference to such proposal :—Notice is therelore hereby given, in purmance of the said Acts, that the said Richard Ingram Danscy will attend at the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Thursday, the Second day of June, 1881, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, to hold a Local Inquiry into the matter aforesaid, when and where all persons interested in the subject of the said Inquiry may attend, and state their objections (if any) to ant order being made by the Local Government Board in conformity with the previsions of the said Acts. Given at the Office of the Local Government Board, at Whitehall, this Fourteenth day of May, 1881. JOHN LAMBERT, Secretary. •

_ THE PRIMROSE.

Sweet Primrose, lovely flower of spring. Thy charms enhanee the vernal scene; What pah te.'s studied art could trace Thy fragile beauty draped in green. The blithesome lark at early morn, Inhales thy breath; then, upward springs, With joyous heart toward the sky. As her matin song she sweetly sings. Thy beauty through the bright snring day. )dates the senses, charms the sight; And in thy scented petal, safe. The glittering dewdrop rests at night. Both old and young alike confess Their love for thee, thou pretty gem. And happy children wanaering stray, To pull thy green and slender stem. 0 how I love thee, pretty flower, What happy memories thou dost give, Sweet memories twined around my heart, And treasured will be, while I live. And when rm gone, of thesis sweet flowers, Shat while I lived such pleasure gave, 0 will kind hands, a garland weave, And place it on the wanderer's grave. J. a. pICILIMISGILL.

He tsats% havingpssshed the journey from Tillie to London in eight days, travelling night and day without stopping, and on his return found awaiting him on his study table the gold medal of the French Geographical Society. H.M.S. Alert, formerly commanded by Sir George Nares, has lately been for some little time in Sydney harbour, but was expected to resume her voyage in April, in order to survey Torres Strait and the various passages used by ves- sels between it and the Deitch islands of the Eastern Archi- pelago. This duty will probably occupy some two years in cornpletion. In his preface to "The Treaty of Ripon," published by the Camden SociAy, the late Mr. Bruce pointed to a con- tinuation of Sir John Borough's notes relating to the nego- tiations between the Scottish and English Commissioners in London during the first months of the Long Parliament as C ; future publication. It is known that these notes are, in one respect, very deficient. They do not give at length the official documents which passed from one side to the other, but merely cite them by their initial words. For- tunately the want can now be filled up,at least as far as the end of March, 1641, by a valuable MS. in the Advocates' Library at Edinburgh, which appears, strange to say, to have escaped the notice of the many admirable publishing societies of Scotland. It is marked 33. 4. 6., and contains the whole ef the correspondence between the Scottish Com- missioners in London anti the committee at Newcastle, ac- companied by the missing documents.—Academy. DISCOVERY OF " FEATHER-ORR" IN THE ISLE OF MAN. —To the last part of the "Transactions" of the Royal Geo- graphical Society of Cornwall, Mr. Warington Smyth, the Crown Inspector of Mines, contributes an interesting de- scription of the occurrences of Plumosite, or Feather-ore, in the Foxdale Mine, Isle of Man. This mine is well known as yielding rich argentiferous lead ores, but it had not been known to contain any antimonial minerals until the recent discovery of plumosite, which is a double sul- phide of lead and antimony. Plumosite is occasionally found in the Hartz, and is there called, from its capillary form, Federerz, but in this country it is a mineral of ex- ceeding rarity. At Foxdale it presents the usual appear- ance of extremely delicate fibres matted together, so as to look almost like a tuft of dark cotton-wool. Under the microscope, however, it is seen to be a reticulation of pris- matic crystals of brilliant metallic lustre. It is curious that other antimonial minerals have not been found in asso- ciation with the plumosite of the Isle of Man. SEWER GASES AND DWELLINGS—Among the most re- cent sanitary appliances which have been pateated is one known as the Antiseptic Apparatus, which has received the commendation of Dr. W. B. Richardson and other competent authorities on questions of hygiene. It is a valuable inven- tion for preventing sewer-gas from entering houses, and it will be appreciated from the simplicity and ingeauity which characterise its construction and operation. The cost brings it within the reach of all classes who care to expend a moderate sum fn the preservation of health, by practically adopting the adage which suggests that "prevention is better than cure," an old saying which is too frequently forgotten. The especial value of this apparatus will be recognised in such places as public offices, hospitals, hotels, and lodging houses, where humanity congregates in num- bers. For private houses its utility is acknowledged by sanitary engineers. The deodorising fluid is permanganate of potash in a coecentrated form, which by its pink colour attests the absence of deleterons matter. When, however, putrescent substances, sewer-gas, or other contaminating matters are present, the fact is made self-evident by a chemical change, altering the colour of the disinfectieg agent, which is said to neutralise the insidious germs of disease. The apparatus is equally available for any ap- proved antiseptic fluid, whether clear or coloured, an ad- ditional advantage which is deserving of consideration. Ample iostruetions are furnished by the manufacturing company, enabling any plumber to fix the appliance, which is automatic in its action ; and the renewal of the fluid once a year, more or less, occupies only a few minutes, and costa from two shillings to half-a-crown. It is placed out of sight; it is not at all likely to get out of order; and from the various facts which have been mentioned it may be ac- cepted aa a most valuable auxiliary to those sanitary pree cautions which are now so urgently pressed upon public attention, and which demand careful consideration on all hands. THE ACTINIC BALANCE —This name has been given pro- visionally by Mr. S. P. Langley, of Allegheny Observatory, to an instrument he has devised for measuring radiant energy, anti which is far more sensitive, prompt, and accu- rate than the best thermopile. Its principle is as follows : Suppose two equal wires to pass from a battery to a differ- ential galvanometer, conveying e•lual currents, one of which tends to move the needle to the right, the other to the left; the needle, thus solicited, remains at zero. It now a ray of some source of radiant energy of higher temperature than the wires fall en one of them, the wire becomes heated, and therefore a worse conductor than before; hence less current names through that wire and the needle is deflected. It was important to get a surface, for exposure-to the radiation, which would have great electric resistance, would show con- siderable change of this for a given change of heat, and would take up and part with heat very quickly. Steel, platinum, and palladium are found die most available metals. Mr. Langley has used fine strips of steel, rolled to the ex- traordinary thinness of 1-300th to 1-500th mm., in which state 8,000 to 12,000 sheets laid one on the other will make but about one inch. Two or more of these, less than half an inch long and 1-20th of an inch wide, are placed side by side in circuit in a small cylinder open at one end, which can be directed to the source of radiant heat. The current used does not warm the strips as much as sdeg. c. above the surrounding temperature. The instrument is stated, roughly, to be five to 100 times as sensitive as the most sen- salve thermopile the author possesses. Mr. Langley gives some examples of its delicacy. Among others, a series of 18 measures of the beat of the moon taken in an hour and a half (under diverse conditions) on November 12th, 1880, with the equatorial of the observatory, using a 13-inch achromatic lens and a smaller condensing lens near the focus. The mean deflection was 41 6. Mr. Langley has been engaged in measurements of nearly homogeneous rays of heat in the diffraction spectrum. His experiments thus far prove the absence of any maxima in the spectrum ; also that the actual solar energy (as it reaches no) is nearly at its minimum precisely where the so-called "actinic curve" is at its maximum. Further, the maximum of heat is found to be not in the ultra-red, but in the orange, while the curve of heat approximately agrees with that of light. The 30th annual report of the above society has just been issued. It takes a more hopeful view with regard to trade prospects as compared with the previous year. The darkest year of the society's existence was 1879, and even at its close, when they were hopefully looking forward to better times, their position was infinitely worse than they found it at the end of 1886. They finished the year 1879 with no lees than 5,028 members on donation or out of work benefit, but since then there had been a gradual improve- ment, the number of unemployed members at the end of last year having fallen to 2,014 There could be no doubt that both the home and foreign trade had very much im- proved during 1880, and there would seem to have been a striking change manifested for the better in oar trade with foreign countries. This improvement in the trade of the country bad also had the effect of materially reducing the number and area of trade disputes, and during the year not a single strike of any moment had occurred. One feature in connection with the great depression and consequent turmoil of 1879 and 1880 which deserved mention had been the exodus of skilled workmen from this country. Bow they now stood as a society might be briefly stated. At the close of 1879 they numbered 401 branches. Since then they had opened new ones at Newcastle-on-Tyne, Sunder- land, Philadelphia. and Worcester, U.S. Thus they had, at the end of 1880, 405 branches, there being in England 203, Scotland 41, Ireland 14, Australia 9, Canada 6, New Zealatel 4, Queensland 1, India 1, United States 32, Malta 1, Turkey 2, and France 1. The approximate number of members at the end of 1879 was 44,087, but at the end of 1880 the total had risen to 44,692, but this figure did not allow for a large number of members on travel, and their entire membership reig,ht be fairly estimated in round numbers at 45,000. Im- proving trade had had its effect in increasing the number Of new members, as during the year 2,979 had been admitted, or 824 more than in the year previous, whilst the exclusions amounted only to 1,765, which was 1 111 less than in 1879. The number of deaths had been 488. The al- tered condition of trade during 1880 and the comparative freedom from disputes rendered fewer levies necessarysand members had only been called upon to pay about 10s, per head in this way, against more than double that amount in 1879. Their =ears still stood at the somewhat high figure of 65. per member, but that was 102 d. less than in thq year preceding. The income for the year had been £128,047, as compared with £135,267 in 1879; but happily the expen- diture for the year was in strong contrast with 1879. Daring 1880 they had spent £139,090, as compared with £245,826 in the previous year. The heaviest item of outlay bad of course been for donation or out-of-work benefit, which claimed £56,580, or £74,198 less than 1879 Sick benefit took £23,295, or a decrease from the year preceding of £9,248. Superannuation expenditure, however, showed tgain a marked increase, and it had risen from £17,730 in 1879 to £20,950 in 1880, the largest rise ever made in one rear. Funeral benefit cost £8,553, which was £B3l lees than in 1879 and £1,321 less than in 1878, which might be regarded satisfactory, as showing the generally improved healthiness of the community. On accident benefit they had spent £1,900, which was rather above the average. The special funds had not been nearly so heavily drawn upon as in 1879, and benevolent grants had fallen from 0,378 in 1879 to £3,473 in 1880; contingent benefit had fallen from C 20,551 to £5,257; and special grants for trade purposes, which in 1879 reached the sum of £18,850, fell last year to £4,305. There had been an excess of expenditure over in- come of £11,043. Their balance at the end of 1879 was 6141,116, and they now had a balance of £130,074, a value oT £2 18s. 20. per member. The Parliamentary session of 1880 had been only signalised brthe passing of the Em- ployers' Liability Act, which, however, would not much eenefit their members, and the most they could hope from it was that it might cause employera to be more careful of she lives and limbs of their workpeople. On the whole, 1880 atlght he looked back upon with a tolerable amount of Betio- faction, for though they came out of it with a reduced balance, it had brought with it much improvement and many changes for the better.

LINES TO LONGFELLOW% The roar of Niagara dies away, The fever heats of war and traffic fade, While the soft twilight melts the glare of day In this new Helicon, the Muses' glade. The roof that sheltered Washington's retreat. Thy home of homes, America, I find In this memorial Mansion, where we greet The full-toned lyrist, with the gentle mind. Here have thy chosen spirits met and flowered, Season on season, 'neath magnetic spells Of him who, in his refuge, rose-embowered, Remote from touch of envious passion dwells. Here Concord's sage and Harvard's wit contend, The wise, the true, the learned of the land, Grave thoughts, gay fantasies together blend In genial converse, 'neath his fostering hand. With other fomb than those of mortal guest The house is haunted; visions of the morn, Voices of night that soothe the soul to rest, Attend the shapes, by aery wand reborn. Serene companions of a vanished age, Noiseless they tread the once familiar floors Or, later offspring of the poet's page, Throng the threshold, crowd the corridors. Sweet Preciosa, down the listening stair Flutters expectant where Victorian sings; Evangeline, with cloistral eyes of prayer, Folds her white hands, in shade of angels' wings. Castilian conquesadors pace the hall, Or red-skinned warriors pass the challenge round. Or Minnehaha's laughter, as the fall Of woodland waters, makes a silver sound. Thor rolls the thunders of his fiery vaunt. The answering battle burns in Olaf's eyes, Or love-crowned Elsie lures us with the chaunt That Wird the waved 'neath star-hung Genoan skies. Here grim-faced captains of colonial days Salute the builders of old German rhyme: And choral troops of children hymn the praise Of their own master minstrel of all time. Fair shrine of pure creations! linger long His bright example,. may his fame increase Discord nor distance ever dim his song. Whose ways are pleasantness, whose paths are peace. Nor Hawthorne's manse, with ancient moss bespread, Nor Irving's hollow is with rest so rife, Is this calm haven, where the leaves are shed Hound Indian summers of a golden life. —77 is Death of Thessistscles and other Poems, by lobe Nichol,

LOST, A BOY. He went from the old home hearthstone Only two years ago, A laughing, rollicking fellow, It would do you good to know; Since then wel-xave not seen him, And we say, with a nameless pain, The boy that we knew and loved so We shall never see again. One bearing the name we gave him Comes home to us to-day, But this is not the dear fellow We kissed and sent away. Tall as the man he calls father, With a man's look in his face, Is he who takes by the hearthstone The lost boy's olden place. We miss the laugh that made music. Wherever the lost boy went; This man has a smile most winsome. His eyes have a grave intent. We know he is thinking and planning His way in the world of men, And we cannot help but love him, But we long for our boy again. We are proud of this manly fellow Who comes to take his place With hints of the vanished boyhood In his earnest, thoughtful face And yet comes back the longing For the boy we must henceforth miss, Whom we sent away from the hearthstone For ever with a kiss.

Some children at a dinner table were discussing that which has often troubled the heads of older and wiser per- sons. "Wasn't Adam a good man before he got a wife ?" "Of course he was," answered a little girl. Bow long was be a good man after he got a wife ?" "A very abort time." "What made him a bad man after he got a wife ?" At this juncture a little fellow spoke up," Miss Ann, I can answer that question." " Well, what is it?" "Eve made him at the wrong apple." If anybody thinks that the genuine Yankee has died out, ! he's very much mistaken. That he is still extant is attested bv an inmdent that recently occurred at Granby. A day hail been set to count the teams crossing the new bridge at Holyoke, with a view of assessing the cost on the adjoin- ing towns. Curiously enough, the citizens of Granby, by the advice of a shrewd official, all stayed at home on that day, and not a Granby team wont over. Of course they couldn't tax Granby; she hadn't any teams. A difficulty has arisen in the Presbyterian Church at Cranberry. The Presbytery was convened to hear and ad- just the matter. They met at Cranberry, and the discus- con became very hot, so that a good deal of ascerbity pre- vailed. We think it was good old Dr. Hall, of Princeton, a clergyman who had the happy faculty of saying a word in season, who rose to attempt to pour oil on the troubled waters. " Mr. Moderator," said he, "I rise to offer a reso- lution, which is that a little sugar be put into the Cranberry tart." The effect was to bring in a laugh at the right mo- ment, and thus to check the bitterness that was beginning to gain ground.—Harper's Neu, Monthly. Two gentlemen well known for quickness of wit, one a politician the other a clergyman, were at a gentleman's house in the country, and on Sunday were, of course, to go to church. The former said to the clergyman, " Come, ride with me." But the clerical gentleman preferred to walk. A shower came on just as the carriage overtook the clergy- man, who had started first. The public functionary put his head oat of the window with— How blessed is he who ne'er consents By ill advice to walk! rra which the minister Immediately retorted— Nor stands is sinners' ways, nor sits Where men profanely talk. Gots) Dusr.—A friend should bear his friend's infirmities. —A wise man will be more anxious to deserve a fair name than to possess it; and this will teach him so to live as not to he afraid to die, —A little leak will sink a great ship.—A man shonld never be ashamed to own he has been in the wrong, which is but saying, in other words, that he is wiser than he was yesterday.—A good word is an easy obligation, acid not to speak ill requires only our silence.—'"" sweetest thing on earth is to be forgotten by all with the exception of those who love us. All else brings more trouble than joy, and as soon as we have completed our task here, and fulfilled our mission, the best thing for us to do is to dis- appear altogether. In a Western village an eloquent revival minister, the Rev. Mr. Lee, once preached from the text," Except a man deny himself, and take up the cross, he cannot be my d:ii- cisle." In the congregation were a Dutchman and his Fran, the tatter of whom was a notorious scold. They were deeply touched by Mr. Lee's preaching. After service Mr Lee mounted his horse and started for his evening appoint- ment. After riding some distance he saw a little ahead of him a man trudging along, carrying a woman on his back. The traveller was a small man, the woman large and heavy. Mr. Lee rode up and found that it was the Dutchman carry- ing his scolding wife. "You did tell us," said the Dutch• man, "drat we must take up de cross, or we could not be saved, and dish woman is de greatest cross I have." , Wisn SAYINGS FROM CHINA.—Here are a few Chinese savings handed down for over two thousands years :—Re- gard faithfulness and sincerity as first principles. A good man is serene; a bad man always in har. To see what is right and not to do it IS want of courar,e. Be who offends against heaven has none to whom he can pray. I will not grieve at men's not knowing me I will grieve that Ido not know men. If in the morning you have heard the voice of celestial reason, in the evening you will be fit to die. He who devotes himself to the study of the true and the good with perseverance and without relaxation,derives therefrom great satisfaction. When we see men of worth we should think of equalling them ; when we see men of a contrary character we should turn inwards and examine ourselves.—

Confucius. FASHIONS AND FLowEns.—A writer on fashions says:— The extent to which imitation blossoms are being used ex- ceeds all my powers of de-,cr:ption. Necklaces of (lowers are worn at the throat with high as well as low bodies, and they are arranged in wreaths around the opening. Also combs of dowers, made to correspond, are fixed in the hair ' straight across the back of the head, or jauntily placed at the side. Round wreaths are worn, at,d single 'flowers are lagened low on the left she, ;minediately behind the ear As may be imagin?d, lovers of flowers do not confine them :selves to the use of artificial ones. Last ...2:130T1 fabulou• sums were spent on flower decoration, both for house anr personal adornment. The lavish expenditure on this luau!, .xcewe,' belief, and gave Fists to very severe animadvdrsions brit the taste for exotics and rare costly blooms Is alread giving signs of returning vigour. and the florist's bill torno one of the largest items in the expenses of some households lie quality of Hartley's Damson is unequalled.—ADYT.

_ SCAB IN SIIISP.—A shepherd informs me that be finds the following the most effectual cure for scab in sheep of anything he has ever tried. He obtains the root, stems, and leaves of foxglove, from which he makes a tea; to this is added an equal quantity of lime juice. Placed in a bottle, with a quill through the cork, the affected parts are easily

dressed. - BENEFITS OF ANALYsts.—As an instance of the benefits of farmers' analytical associations, the North British Agri- culturist mentions that a member of thelnvernesa and Black. isle Analytical Association, last year bought six tons of manure at £l3. The analysis showed, however, that the value of the manure supplied was only .£B, the result being that the manure merchant had to refund the farmer £3O, or a sum nearly equal to the entire expenses of the association

during the year. FARMERS AND SECOND-HAND SUPELIES.—It Seems to have become the fashion in modern days for the farmer to get supplies for his family from the baker, butcher, and brewer, instead of getting them from his own stores, and having them prepared on the premises. All tradesmen supply themselves at prime cost with such articles as they deal in. Not so the farmer, he sells hrs sheep to buy back the mutton at an increased price, his wheat comes back to him in the shape of bread after two or three profits have been made, and he parts with the whole of his barley in- stead of malting a part of it. In the winter a family of ordinary size may consume a whole sheep profitably, as the meat may hang for a month or longer, and be all the better i for the process; and during the summer months the appli- cation of the co-operative principle among two or three neighbours would enable them to kill and divide in turns a sheep or lamb amongst them. In the home manufacture of bread 30 or 40 per cent. may be saved • and what is nicer and sweeter than a home-made loaf, and yet this involves, in many cases, too much trouble, and the young ladies do not like the pork. " PRESERVING FARMERS' WIVES."—A lady to whom was assigned" Preserving" as the subject of an essay to be read at the meeting of a county grange in Missouri instead of giving the proportion of various compotes of fruit and sugar, very sensibly goes to the root of the matter, and ad- vises farmers' wives to preserve themselves. She says : ,6 We have seen a great many kinds of preserves, but we have the first well-preserved farmers' wife yet to see. There are well-preserved old maids and bachelors. We have heard of the latter being pickled, but have never seen a specimen, though it strikes us they would make a better pickle thaa preserve. But the poor tired farmer's wife never finds time to preserve herself. It is always peaches, pears, plums, drc., standing over the hot stove all the time. If it were not for stopping to take the baby now and then, she would certainly be in perpetual motion, and all this just to tickle the palate of her liege lord and his male friends, for certainly woman's alimentive bump is so benumbed while standing over the steaming, roasting mess of conglomerated victuals that she has no appetite for the same when done. Now we come before you with a recipe to preserve farmers' wives. Never worry; take all the rest that is needed to recuperate your strength, that has been wasted over the preserving pan. Get you a washing machine, a sewing machine, and an organ. Read, and keep yourself posted, so that you can talk with your husband; have something new to tell him, and do not always be under the constrained duty of keeping silent and learning of him. Go to all the public gatherings with him. This gives you the change that is so much needed. Do not think you cannot spare the time. If he can, you certainly can. You will find it will add years to , your youth and health. According to statistics, there are ' more farmers' wives in the insane asylums than of any other class. This is simply because there is not enough change in their lives, as they' have but one round of duties to be gone through with, year in and year out. We have read that you could put a sane person in a walled-up.room and confine him there, and he would soon become insane; and we have come to the conclusion that it is the want of this change that drives farmers' wives to insanity. The average farmer's wife has not even reading matter provided for her. The farmer generally takes a paper that gives the markets and his political views. This satisfies him; and he never takes a thought but what it is all-sufficient for her. There are very few women who have been educated to take an in- terest in politics, and they should have something suited to their tastes. We heard a farmer's wife say not long since that she had never read a word in a newspaper since she had been a married woman. If that woman is preserved physically, she certainly is not mentally. Farmers' wives, take more time to preserve yourselves, and let some of the other preserving go. Your families will be just as healthy, and you will be better able to serve them.—Bell's Weekly Messenger.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

SHOW PINTS AT HOHlL.—There is .a saying so fermu.. as to have passed into a popular proverb, that "Charity 'should begin at home." However this may be, there is a divine precept about piety, which is plain and easily under- stood—namely, that piety should begin at home. The re- ference was first to filial duty, but reaches through all the relations of life. There are men, and still oftener women, who ready to think they have a vocation, or a "mission" of some sort or other—in the church it may be, or in the school, the hospital, or other public position. Perhaps some of them have such a call, but the apostle reminds us of other and earlier duties, and more imperatively demanding atten- tion. These first, he said, those afterwards; "These ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone." Paul would have had very little patience with the people who rush here and there to "services" to hear a favourite preacher—as others are hurrying hither and thither to hear a favourite singer—if the while there was a pile of work left undone at home, or left for other fingers wearied with work to do. And Paul's Master might be made angry (for angry Ile sometimes was) by the sight of effusive sym- pathy shed in sighs, and tears, and gold, over suffering strangers, while a pining sister " in weariness often" had to drag on many a lonely hour, perhaps in a sick room, seldom cheered by the presence or loving help of those who are busy out of doors instead of first showing piety at home. Sunday at Home. Otrramann JUSTICR.—If there ever existed a man whose bosom was pervaded by a sense of justice, it was a justice of the peace in Otsego County, who, ordinarily correct in his deportment, in one unguarded moment omitted his cus- tomary cold water, and roamed into the fields of Bacchus. He became a boozy J.P., and next morning had the result- ing headache. He became disgusted with himself, and re- solved not only to make an expiation, bat to vindicate the outraged law. At the usual hour he entered his office, for- mally opened court, called his own name as defendant in a suit for having violated a certain statute, and then asked the prisoner what he had to say. In the role of prisoner he pleaded guilty to the offence, said it was a shame for a man of his years and position, but hoped "the court" would not be too severe on him, as he was determined to reform. "The prisoner will stand up," said the stern old justice. Then the prisoner arose. " Now," said the justice, "I am very sorry you have been brought into this court on a charge which so seriously affects your good name And standing in society. You have set a bad example, and if you go on at this rate you will bring sorrow and disgrace on yourself and family. I sentence you to pay a fine of ten dollars and costs, or to thirty days' imprisonment in the county jail" The" prisoner" said he would prefer to pay the fine; and when the court closed he walked over to the poor-master of the town and paid the ten dollars.—Harper's New Monthly. DIET AND FEVEIL—A writer in Chambers' Journal says that Dr. Oswald, formerly director of the City Hospital, at Very Cruz, in an article "On the relation of Diet to Yellow Fever." endeavours to prove that the disease is produced by diet and not by climate. "The so-called hotbeds of disease along the coast of South America," he writes, "are remark- able for the frequency rather than the destructiveness of I their epidemics. In Vera Cruz, for instance, the outbreak of 'an undoubted indigenous yellow fever epidemic between the first of July and the middle of August is an annual phe- nomenon; but the experience of a full century has proved that the plague confines itself to four generally not very numerous classes. These are foreigners front North America and Europe, anti their black or Indian servants, who imi- tate their habits." "The native citizens of Vera Cruz," continues Dr. Oswald, "would ridicule the contagiousness of yellow fever. Not philanthropists only. but idle ladies and children visit that city hospital and the houses of fever- stricken foreigners. From the mouth of the Rio Grande to the delta of La Plata, neither physicians nor laymen enter- tain the slightest doubt about the origin of idiopathic fevers, but refer them to dietetic abuses as unhesitatingly as we as- cribe dyspepsia to the same cause." A contrast is then made of the flesh diet and stimulating drinks of the foreigner, and the diet of fruit, vegetables, and water of the native. The immunity of the latter is pointed out, and the Doctor thus concludes :—" If we would ascertain the antecedents of those families or classes of our population who furnished the largest quota of typhus and yellow fever patients, and of those who enjoyed the most conspicuous immunity, the comparison of their respective dietetic records would con- vince us that the contagions principle discriminates in the choice of its victims, alai that there is no such thing as a -edemic disease"

A dwelling-house in Notting Rill took fire on Monday. The flames spread so quickly that escape by the lower rooms was immediately cut off, and six persons were burnt to death. A man in Howard county slept 24 hours waiting for day- light to appear. His house had been entirely nowed in, a fact of which he was not aware until a neighbour went down the chimney and explained to him the situation. It took him two hours to shovel out. Mr. R. L. Bruges, of Melksham, a magistrate for Glouces- tershire, was brought up at Marlborough-street Police Court, on Monday, charged with writing and publishing a false and scandalous libel concerning the Countess of Lans- dale. The libel was contained in a letter written to the Earl of Lonsdale, who found it awaiting him on his return from America. The defendant was remanded. An attempt was made a few minutes before midnight on Monday to blow up the Liverpool Central Police Station. A loud report was heard, and on inquiry being made it was found that a tube of some explosive material, supposed to be gun-cotton or dynamite, had been thrown into the door- way of the Police Station. A large number of windows were shattered, but fortunately no personal injury was sus- tained. While one of the customs lockers was on duty the other day in a bond in Timber-bush, Leith, he saw a serpent slowly emerging from a bale of cork. He immediately seized the dangerous reptile, and killed it by pouring brandy on its head. On being examined it proved to be of a very venomous kind, and measured about two feet Rang. It is supposed to have been revived by the heat. Mr. Hibbert, M.P., Secretary to the Local Government Board, writing to the Oldham Trades Council, says he agrees with them that our Government should decline to negotiate a new treaty with France unless it is based upon the prin- ciple of a !general reduction of present duties, or, at the worst, of the maintenance of the present system. In any case he trusts that there may be no attempt to impose re- taliatory duties on French goods. At Bradford, on Tuesday, the bench inflicted the full penalty of £2OO on Sidney Green, in whose house in Brad- ford an illicit still in full working order was discovered in March last. Green managed to escape from the house through a window, and has not yet been apprehended. He had several times previously been convicted of a like offence,' and in addition to imposing a heavy fine the magistrates granted a warrant for his apprehension. • The sentence of death passed en Albert Moore, a young soldier, for the wilful murder of an old woman named Marsh, at Gravesend, on the ICth February, was carried out on Tuesday morning inside Maidstone Prison, at eight o'clock, by Marwood, in the presence of a few officials and three representatives of the press. The con- demned man, who has expressed great penitence since his conviction,walked firmly to the scaffold. He was allowed a drop of eight feet, and struggled slightly after falling. The black flag was immediately hoisted over the gaol gates for the space of one hour. Addressing a meeting of the leading traees unionists of North-East Lancashire, at Blackburn, on Saturday, Mr. Broadhurst, M.P., said the main object of the Employers and Workmen's Act of last session was to cause employers to exercise greater care in the selection of managers, in regard to the quality of plant, and in the supervision of ' works, and that the object would lee defeated by the substi- tution of an annual contribution by employers to common I fund for the payment of compensation to injured workpeople , for the liability of employers under the Act. He hoped an I amendment Act would soon be passed to prevent employers' contracting themselves out of the provisions of the Act. The legal proceedings in connection with the services at • St. Vedast's Church, Foster-lane, have at length led to the sequestration of the living by the Bishop of London. Within the last few days an official notice to that effect, signed by the Bishep, has been placed on the doors of the church. In this notice the Bishop appoints the church- wardens as sequestrators, and directs them to receive and I hold all emoluments appertaining to the living for the benefit of the new vicar hereafter to be appointed. The document states that the Bishop has been induced to fequestrate the living in consequence of the cession of the late vicar' the Rev. T. Pelham Dale, who has now been Inducted by the Bishop of Lincoln into a living in that diocese. The Revised Translation of the New Testament was issued to the public on Tuesday. This is the first and most Important instalntent of that new revision of the Authorised Versii n of the Bible, which has been proceeding at West- minster for the past ten years. At the Cannon-street Hotel, at a public breakfast, largely and influentially attended, in connection with the 82nd anniversary of the Religious, Tract Society, the Lord Mayor, who presided, was presented by Dr. Manning, in the name Of the institution, with a copy of the Revised New Testament, which was to belaid upon the table of Convocation, and a copy handed to Her Majesty prior to its general circulation. The Archbishop of Canterbury representing the Committee of Revisers of the New Testament, arrived' at Windsor Castle, yesterday after- noon, for the purpose of presenting to Her Majesty a copy of the newly-revised Testament. The Archbishop was accompanied by Miss Tait. Mr. J. T. Hibbert, M.P., writing to a constituent at Old- ham, says that the question raised by the exclusion of Mr. Bradlaugh has, been to him one of great constitutional im- port.. He was not concerned with the hon. member's opinions, but with the question whether, a constituency having elected him, the House of Commons was justified in excluding him on account of his opinions from the due ful- filment of his legal rights and duties. Mr. Lyulph Stanley, M.P., writing on the subject of the Land Bill, expresses regret that the rules of debate which when framed were used in good faith and honouraliy, are being abused for the purpose of obstructing the work of legislation. There is required, he says, not "urgency," but such a change in the standing orders "as will give to the majority its proper power of doing its work with fair discussion, but without obstruction." A great many observers of the proceedings in Parliament will agree with Mr. Stanley in this con- I elusion. TIM PRINCESS OF WALES ON FEES TRAMS AND PROTEC- TION.—The Princess of Wales has been presented with two shawls by the Associated Chambers of Agriculture, with a memorial urging her Royal Highness to adopt the use of fabrics of home-grown wool, with the view of thereby assist- ing the depressed state of agriculture, especially in York- shire. In reply, a letter has been received from Mr. Holz- mann, the Princess's secretary, stating that she did not think the result aimed at was to be brought about simply by her wearing articles of home-made manufacture and growth, for in recent years ehe had used woollen fabrics more largely than formerly. She was inclined to believe that the present depression proceeded from a variety of economic. commer- cial, and other circumstances, many of them closely con- nected with the conflicting questions of free trade and protection. The annual meeting of the Peace Society was held on Tuesday, Mr. Arthur Pease presiding. Mr. Henry Richard, M.P., read an abstract of the report, which dwelt with satis- faction on the cessation of the Transvaal war, and on the reception given to Mr. Richard's two motions in the House of Commons. Mr. Caine, Ml'., in moving the adoption of the report, said Mr. Gladstone had always been in favour of arbitration and restitution, and among the brightest jewels in the crown of that great statesman were the restoration of the lonian Islands to Greece, the settlement of the Alabama claims, the withdrawal from Afghanietan, and the act of justice to a weaker power in the face of defeat in South Africa. Mr. Illingworth, M.P., moved a resolution, express- ing approlaation of the action of the Government in Afghan- istan and the Transvaal. Sir Wilfrid Lawson, in seconding the motion, referred to the dispute between France and Tunis, which be said showed that the old spirit of military I glory was not dead ma the other side of the channel. The best way for England to keep the peace was to " boycott " the army, and refuse to join its ranks. THE EXTRAORDINARY VACCINATION SCARES IN THE BLACK CoutrrEv.—On Friday afternoon, the rumour that the "black doctors" were about to visit the board schools and vaccinate the children reached the upper part of West Bromwich, and Mayer's-green Board Schools were besieged with angry parents demanding their children. It was stated in the crowd that six "black doctors" bad been seen to enter the approach to the schools, and, stimulated by this extra- ordinary assertion, about 50 women, with their sleeves up- turned, ran up the entrance to the schools and demanded their children. The school doors were made fast, and Mr. Perkins, master of the Queen-street boys' school, was sent for. When the messenger arrived at Queen-street a similar scene presented itself. The schools were surrounded by 300 men and women, who asked that their children might be ant home. Unable to satisfy the mob, upon reaching Mayer's-green Schools, Mr. Perking found that the parents assembled had become so exasperated, that they had forced their way into the schools and were carrying off their inl dd hours considerable disturbance prevailed at most of the screaming chmeidladenrdednteod. schools in the town and district. In Weduesbury, some "dialect" tp'Codeee r ei in theld Blackbe given Country n n to them, as they objected to have their offspring "cut to pieces by black men, Mr. Gladstone, or anyone else." It was found necessary at the principal schools to dismiss the children and close the schools for the day. The greatest iniechief in connection with the matter is, that the examina- tions are just on, and it is utterly spoiling the chances of good' Government grants. AN INLAND PARCEL Posy.—The Postmaster General and officials have recently been arranging the details of an in- land 'parcel post. It is stated that a parcel stamp, the form of which has been approved, will be issued, the maximum being 6d. For the present the maximum weight to be trans- mitted will be 41b. Parcels will be received at any post- office in England, Scotland, and-Ireland, and trasmitted to any address being in connection with the International hhlee tvs schools, Several their children fainted, and for two Parcel Post, arrangements for which have been already announced. The railway companies will receive as their share of the cost of the carriage ball the amount given to the Post-office for transmiasion, the proportions being ad- justed by the Railway Clearing-house. The parcels will not be received during the whole time that post-offices are open, but will be limited to the hours for transacting registration bueinems. The parcels will not as a rule be carried by the night mail trains. The task of distribution is the most for- tnidable difficulty. In London and the larger provincjal towns this wjli be effected by special carts, but in the country districts the ordinary letter carriers will have to be burdened with the parcels. This, however, will, it is believed, be iatisfactorily arranged. It is intended that the parcel post shall commence next October. If parliamentary powers are necessary they will be incorporated in the bill which will have to be obtained enabling sixpenny telegrams to be started on the first day of next year, which Act will also .4ive special powers in relation to the telepbone.—Peil Mall Gazette.

LORD PALMERSTON. When the Derby-Disraeli Administration collapsed in 1859, Lord Palmerston arose from his temporary fall like a giant refreshed, and for the remaining six years of his life reigned supreme in Downing-street. This period does not stand out as remarkable in the annals of our history for grand legisla- tive achievements. His lordship, it is true, carried us through the dangers of the Italian War, riveted us, through the Treaty of Commerce, in a closer alliance with France, carried out Reforms in India that led to its comparative prosperity, remodeled our bankruptcy and our educational systems, and steered through the difficulties of the American War and the Polish Rebellion; but pursuing at home a policy of " masterly inactivity," he did not enrich the Sta- tute Book with any grand reforms—such as those which Sir Robert Peel and Mr. Gladstone have accomplished. In concluding our sketches of Lord Palmerston, we intend this week to look at his career as a whole and pronounce judgment thereon, by no means an easy task. His Ministry was so thoroughly one of transition, and the influence which he exercised on our domestic politics was sol individual in character, beginning and ending in himself, that it is some- what difficult to do his lordship full justice. He was not thoroughly identified with any of the two great Parties. As Sir Henry Bulwer happily says in the appreciative and discriminating sketch with which he introduces his bio- graphy—" He was behind the eager, but before the slow." Hence it followed that he was much more liberal in his foreign than in his home policy, and though his desire to ad- vance the interests of constitutional freedom on the Con- tinent necessarily led him to ally himself with the party of progress, he never entered earnestly into their views for the extension of popular power at home. His death was the beginning of a new political era in this country. It let loose pent up forces which had been chafing against the restraint under which he had held them, it transformed the character of the Party of which he had been the nominal leader, and brought to the front men of a much more energetic and de- termined spirit ; it ended the reign of "masterly inactivity," and inaugurated a period of advance in which the changes have been so marked and rapid that we already feel our- selves removed by a long interval from the pleasant and easy-going statesman who so long baffled the hopes of more ardent reformers. Since we commenced our studies on "Her Majesty's Prime Ministers" we are free to confess that our opinion of Lord Palmerston's character has undergone some change. The standing reproach against him has been that he trimmed his sails to every breeze, that he was only con- sistent in the retention of office—that he was fixed only to the Treasury Bench—that his principle was that of the Vicar of Bray, and the length of time during which he he'd office, and the diverse character of the Administrations in which he served at first gave countenance to the charge. It is not easy to see how a man could have acted under such inveterate Tories of the narrowest and most tigoted school, as Lord Liverpool and Mr. Percival; under the milder and more liberal Canning; and then under the harsher regime of Wellington, and afterwards under such decided reformers as Lord Grey, Lord Melbourne, and Lord Russell, without losing consistency and self-respect. But, singular as it may seem, a closer inspection of the facts removes a good deal of the impression produced by their bare' recital, and our esti- mate of Lord Palmerston ,as a statesman and as a man is raised by a more intimate knowledge of his character and policy. In Lord Palmerston there was, at all events, no violent change, no sudden and inexplicable transfer of allegiance from one party to the other. Everywhere we find in him the keenest sense of personal honour, and a fixed determination to do nothing by which it might even seem to be compromised. His separation from the Tories was the consequence of his strong sympathy with Canning, and the final rupture with them was hastened by the ungenerous, not to say unfair, conduct of the Government, of which he was a member, in connection with the Cambridge election. In truth, the , politician of those days who had so far emanc; /rated himself from the Tory creed as to pronounce in favour of the receg- nition of the Roman Catholic claims, had already taken a step in advance, the ultimate result of which was sure to be a severance from the old Tories. As a Canningite, Lord ' Palmerston was eminently loyal to the name and principles of the great statesman, and in the difficulties which led to the cecession of Mr. Huskisson and others from the Wellington Government, no one acted a more manly and straightforward part. The course he took then in relation to the transfer of the seats at Penrlivn and Elea- ford to such constituencies as Manchester and Birmingham, I which the shortsighted bigots of the Party, with the Duke I among them and Sir Robert Peel tacitly assenting, were con- tent to leave without representatives at all, prepared the way for his alliance with Earl Grey and the Wiligs in carry- ing the Reform Bill. From the time of his entering the Grey Cabinet no one could accuse him of infidelity to Party obligations, though many felt that on one or two occ tsions he pushed personal aonaiderations too far, and others de- sired that his allegiance to Liberal principles had been more thorough-going and hearty. We must, however, look at him as he was, not as we should have wished him to be, and a dispassionate judge can hardly deny that there was that in his peculiar temperament and mode of looking at questions which fitted him to do service to the country in the transition period during whin he held the reigns of power. A moderate politician, he was one who was not in- clined to change imerely for the sake of maintaining theoretical consistency, but who looked rather to practical results, and, if these were good, cared little for the viola- tion of abstract principles; one who allowed considerations of expediency to enter largely into his judgment of poli- tical questions, and this itself may serve to explain the difference between the Party relations of his early and his later days. Quick to perceive the direction in which the current of ideas impelled the nation, be followed it at times slowly, rarely anticipated it, and never attempted to turn it back. One might compare his conduct to the "Times," but a selfseeker, a mere intriguer, a trickster he was not. One marked characteristic of Lord Palmerston was hie facetiousness and good humour. On his first becoming Prime Minister his conduct of affairs in the House of Com- mons was condemned for levity of tone and misplaced jocu- larity. Let him remain Premier for a year or two, observed a Member of the highest literary and political distinction, and our standard will be lowered till we prefer thislaughing, I devil-may-care method of getting through business to the wit of Canning and the gravity of Peel. But Lord Palmer- ston—whose levity was on the surface, and useful as well as justifiable against established bores—rose with each succeed- ing Session and on great occasions was rarely found want- ing in moral influence or in the dignity befitting his posi- tion. His alleged carelessness was the ease of a consum- mate master of his craft. He wielded his weapon With hand whose almost careless coolness spoke Its grasp well used to deal the sabre stroke. His play of mind was equally edifective in catching and im- proving any passing drollery or humorous thought. When Lord Derby's Translation of the Illiad was first an- nounced, a guest at Broadlands told him he must keep pace with his great rival by translating the Enied. "Stop till I am out .of office, and the parallel will be complete," was his lordship's reply. On one occasion he laughingly quoted the authority of an eminent physician, that continuance in office, with the resulting employment, was good for the health. "Would not active opposition do as well ?" in- quired a friend. ', Certainly not,' replied Lord Palmerston, "that stirs up the bile and creates acidity. Ask Disraeli if It does not." "Put a little more starch into your neck- cloth, my dear —" he said once to a favourite diplomatist, who he thought did not hold up his head high enough at the Courtwhere the Minister represented us. This humour added much to his popularity, and was to him a source of strength. Besides Lord Palmerston was an Englishman to the back- bone, and nothing but an Englishman. The cosmopolitan traits of Canning, the honourable Liberalism of Russell, were wanting in him. Peel and Gladstone were in every respect his antipodes. In the purest sense of the word, he was a patriot. Throughout his long and faithful service to the State, his one object was to uphold English interests, to jealously maintain the prestige of England, and on all neces- sary occasions to assert the authority and influence of Eng- land. The interest of England, he said, was his Polar star. And during an unusually lengthened political career, what- ever were the errors he fell into, he never allowed English , interests to be put in jeopardy, or a sickly sentimentality or I an unworthy ambition to obscure his view of what was best for the welfare of the country. In the long retrospect of such a career, many acts may be found the expediency of which may now appear doubtful, but none which can im- peach the singleness of his policy or the purity of his motives. That he believed to the utmost in England and her proud destiny; that he was, as Earl Russell said, "the Minister of no country but England ;" that he "bore on high the red cross shield" in the stormy as in the sunshiny hour ; that he was ever ready to make the will of the nation known, no matter who frowned upon her—all this is ad- mitted, and all this is much, and it is this which the his- torian will delight to tell. On the list of her Majesty's Prime Ministers he will be remembered as he himself would have wished to be remembered—not as the greatest, but as the most English of our Statesmen. He died on Wednesday, October 25th, 1865, at the ripe age of 81, and on Friday, November 3rd, the mortal remains of the great Premier were laid in the north transept of Westminster Abbey, where his dust will mingle with that of the Pitts, Cannings, Wilberforce, Charles James Fox, and others whose labours for our country's weal resembled his own. He was laid near to the Senate Hall, where he chacked the passions of debate and swayed the rivalries of pirties with a sagacity and success surpassed by none of his fellow sleepers in the grand old abbey. His name will not be transmitted to history as the author of any great measure or of any permanent policy. Much that he laboured to construct has already disappeared; nor did he found a school of politicians to perpetuate the maxims of his Government. He was contented to serve his generation and to accept its confidence as his highest reward, and his career, judged by his own standard, must be deemed successful. After a long life of perpetual activity, enjoyed with a relish. which is itself always a source of popularity and a propitiation of human affection, be died surrounded by friends, and ,arely perhaps did a man who in his time exasperated such a variety of feelings and made for himself a host of tem- porary enemies, pass into the " eternal silenstes " so generally respected and so sincerely mourned.

THE TENANT FAEMEn'S CATECHISM. I

The following is a copy of a remarkable document which had an extensive circulation some time ago among the tenant farmers in Ireland : What is your name ? My family name was originally Man, bat through fraud, injustice, and usurpation of my birthright I became depen- dent on my master Tenanny, and in my servitude am known among my compeers as the Victim of Oppression. Who were the immediate cause of this change of name to a servile cognomen, and also of the condition to which you are now doomed ? My Landlord, and his Agent, brought it about in the days of my ancestors; and hence from my youth I was made a child of sorrow and an inheritor of a bundle of raga. What did your Landlord and his Agent then do for you when you became a subordinate to their power, whether in your youth or in your manhood? They did promise and vow three things in my name— Firstly, that I should renounce all the comforts of this life. and all the pleasures found therein; secondly, that I should be a hewer of wood and drawer of water ; and, thirdly, that I should be a slave for them all the days of my life—a mere chattel of their household and drudge on their estate. Do you not think you are bound to believe, in your con- science, and do as they promised for you? No, verily; and by God', help I will endeavour to shake off the chains by which lam bound, and better my condition socially and materially, and strive to continue in the same till my life's end. Rehearse the articles of your belief. I believe that God is no respecter of persons; that He is , King of Kings and Lord of Lords; and that every man should enjoy the fruits of his labour, for the labourer is worthy of his hire. I also believe that Ide not enjoy the fruit of my labour, for I am compelled against nature to give it to men who reap where they do net sow and gather where they have not strewn, who are better known in the banqueting hall, the foreign club house, or the betting field than in the school of industry, or amongst their honest, hard-worked, and careworn tenantry, save when the corn is ripe, I also believe that lam not able to pay my rent from the produce of my farm, and that the pomp and vanity of those men, who, like birds of passage, leave when they get the last grain of corn—men who live in ease and indolence, rolling about in purple and fine linen, and faring sump- tuously every day on the toil and sweat of their fellow creatures, and revelling on the bread of idleness—have reached their highest climax, and that it is full time they should be brought to know and feel that the stalwart and industrious farmers are the bone and sinew of the land on which they toil as slaves, and that they will no longer en- dure or submit to the burdens heaped upon them by a class of extravagant harpies, called landlords, who are the chief cause of the grievances ond disturbances in this country. I believe in the fall of rents, the lowering of taxes, the sup- preesionof crime, and the emancipation of all serfs—whether social or political—from the domination of the privileged few. What do you chiefly learn in the articles of your belief just enumerated? First, I learn that justice demands such a state of things to cease, that rents must fall, and that tenant-right must be carried to the satisfaction of the people, no matter what Government rules or who wields the sceptre. Secondly, that honest, independent men must be sent out to value the land on equitable principles, and a fair price laid on accord- ing to quality, whether in the interest of the nation or in that of territorial proprietors, and that landlords are not en- titled to benefits arising from the improvement of the soil, as all is owing to the labour of the industrious farmer; and, further, that proper security must be given to the tenant farmer that he or his heirs cannot be removed so long as they pay their rents and conduct themselves as becometh honest and peaceful membei a of society. Thirdly, that all claeees will go hand in hand and stand shoulder to shoulder in this legal warfare, and never give up till they bring landlord and tenant on a closer basis of equality; and, if need be, stand there, opponents face to face with tyranny, in the hour of battle; for he who would not fight for his ;ights and his daily bread would not fight for his sovereign no, he true to his country in its hour of need. You said that year landlord and hie agent did bind yeu to keep all their laws and commandments. Tell me how many there are. Ten, and en addendum. Which be they ? The SIITIP which they spoke of in their office when they brought. me out of the region of peace into a veritable land of bondage. R ineet them. "let. Thou !bait have no tenant-right. "nil. Thou shalt not make to thyself any charges on thy farm, nor buy nor sell, without our consent, nor com- plain egainq any of us er ours for rearing game thereon for our own amusement or coursing days, nor keep dog nor gun nor cat, nor any living animal to disturb them in any way, no matter what damage thou mayst sustain thereby; thou shalt bow down and pay obeisance unto us, for we are thy landlords, and jealous ones, who shall visit thee and thy children with heavy rents, notices, and ejectment processes if thou disobey us, or neglect to pay thy rents. "3rd. Thou shalt not take the name of thy landlord nor his agent in vain, nor speak slightly of us, no matter whet we do; for we will not hold them guiltless who take our name in vain. "4th. Remember thou arta tenant-at-will; 364 days shalt thou labour and do all that thou haat to do, but the first day of November in each year is our rent day, in which thou shalt do no manner of work till thou reachest our office, and payest us to the uttermost farthing. "sth. Honour thy landlord and his agent, with hat in hand, and be punctual in thy payments, so that thy days may be long in the farm which we let onto thee to till and reap for our profit. "6th. Thou shalt not kill nor appropriate any of our game. " 7lh. Thou shalt not commit thyself by violating any of our rules, or by disobeying any of our imperative com- mands, even to the obeying of our whippers-in or bailiffs on our estate. 'Bth. Thou shalt not cut down nor remove any of our trees or turbery, no matter what thy wants may be, or how they may inconvenience thee, for-all that grows thereon is ours, no matter who planted them. "9th. Thou shalt not murmur nor complain against us, nor expose our misdoings in courts of law or through the public press, but endure all with patience forbearauce, and long suffering, so that thou mayst be called a profitable ser- vant and a meritorieus subordinate. "10th. Thou shalt not covet thy landlord's house; thou shalt not covet thy landlord's wife, nor his footman, ncr his maids, nor his asses, nor anything that is his, though all is supported and procured by the toil, the sweat, and privation of his tenantry. "11th. Thou shalt understand that thy landlord bath power to add to the Decalogue, and be hereby addeth another commandment to the same, is wit :—lnasmuch as it seemeth good unto him to enjoin thee, as an obedient tenant, that thou shalt in all cases give thy vote to thy lanclhad, or to his nominee, as seemeth best for him to de- cide, so that he or hie rominee may be duly returned to Par- liament, in order to make new and more stringent laws to bind tenants and subordinate persons to observe the sacred rights of property, and pay due homage to their territorial lords; to be subrniseive to them in all things, and bow to their exalted dignity which God bath raised that they may be princes in the land and anointed ones, born to rule and revel in the great inheritances He bath eet apart for his favourites in Israel. Thus thou shalt do all the days thou art permitted to live, and praise the Lord that thine eyes have seen the grandeur of their state, and the exceeding , glory of their power. itan

TYNDALL'S REMINISCENCES— OP CAJILYLII. Professor Tyndall writes :—I do not know what Carlyle's aptitudes in the natural history sciences might have been, but in regaid to physics the contrast between him and Goethe was strik- ing in the highest degree. His opinions had, for the most part, taken their final set before the theory of man's descent was enunciated, or, rather, brought within the domain of true causes by Mr. Darwin. For a time he abhorred the theory, as tending to weaken that ethical element in man which, in Carlyle's estimation, as in that of others, transcends all science in importance. But a softening, if not a material, change, of his 'views was to be noticed later on. To my own knowledge, he approved cordially of certain writings in which Mr. Darwin's views were vigorously advo- cated, while a personal interview with the great naturalist caused him to say afterwards that Charles Darwin was the most charming of mi n. Carlyle was sternly real, but he was a gentleinan—full of dignity and delicacy of thought and feeling. No finer courtesy could be shown by man than was shown by him to the ladies who visited him in his modest home at Chelsea. I see him now, standing bareheaded in his sober dressing-gowl on the pavement below his door- steps, with the sun shining on his grey heirs, saying the last kind and courteous words to a. lady whom his three-and- eighty years did not prevent hem from conducting down- stairs. Knowing the depth of Carlyle's tenderness, I should almost feel it to be bathos to cite the cases known to no which illustrate it. I call to mind his behaviour towards some blind singers in the streets of Marseilles, and the in i terest he took n the history of a little boy whom, during my momentary separation from him, he found lying in the shadow of a tree and over whose limbs paralysis was slowly creeping. There was a kind of radiance in the sorroW pieced in in the old man's face as he listened to the tale, arel.' probably looked to the woes beyond it. The self-same radi- ance I saw for the last time as he lay upon his sofa and for some minutes rested his head upon my shoulder a few week 6 before hi a death. Ido not expect to see the like of it again. "Give your life royally," was his exhortation to the re- former eight-and-thirty years ago. In such fashion Carlyle gave his own life to his 'country and to mankind. England may forget this for the moment, but she will renaem . ber h- and by.

FORSTF.R.—ANOTHER SCENE.— Mr. HEALY asked if it was true that the police at Ennis- corthy recently tore down placards calling upon Wexford men to "assemble in thousands to witness landowners degraded, the collection of unjust rents, and the resources of buckshot Forster liberally supplied to enforce justice, kc." and did the Government sanction the action of the police?— Mr. FORT= replied that it was true the placards were posted summoning the people to assemble in thousands at I the Wexford Court House, and he thought the police had acted perfectly right. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. O'Doemata wished to know if their action was induced and approved of, because the words "Buckshot Forster" appeared in the placards ? (Oh, oh.)—Mr. FORSTER, in reply, was cheered as he said he considered it no part of his duty to reply to questions addressed to him for purposes of insult.—Mr. HEALY then rose again, and moved the adjournment of the House. (Oh, oh.) He declared that he had no intentionof insult, and that this was the only case of bringing these matters forward. If the Chief Secretary continued in this fashion to support the police in their arbitrary conduct he would find the outrages ten times the number they now are. (01, oh.)—Mr. O'DowerEaa followed, and seconded the motion. He also disclaimed any idea of insult. Chief secretarieswere often known by epithets not complimeetary. For instance a former Chief Secretary was once called "Orange Peel."—Mr. FORSTER rose to reply, and was re- ceived with cries of "No, no," from the Ministerial benches. I The plaintiff in Clarke v. Bradlaugh, applied on Monday to the Queen's Bench Division, for leave to sign judgment and issue execution against the defendant for the enormous tines to which he is liable, for having eat and voted in Parliament without having taken the oath or made affirma- tion. Mr. Bradlaugh took a 'technical objection, which ' depended upon the dates given respectively in the writ and the statement of claim, and argued that the action was not maintainable because it appeared that the cause of action arose after the issue of the writ. The argumerts were not concluded at the rising of the court.—Further argument in the case of Clarke v. Bradlaugh,was continued on Tuesday murning at Westminster, before Lord Coleridge and Mr. Justice Bowen, on the motion by the plaintiff for judgment and execution against the defendant for having sat and voted in the House of Commons without taking the oath. The courtroom was crowded. Mr. Bradiaugh resumed hie contention that the issuing of the writ was a judicial act, and that no cause of action had arisen. Mr. Bradlaugh's. argument had proceeded but an hour when the further heas- ing unexpectedly collapsed. The defendant said he doubted as a question of fact whether he had voted when the writ was issued. There being no question of fact on the record, Mr. Giffard asked leave to traverse the statement of claim as to the fact whether be had voted. Leave was given ac- cordingly, and the case was adjourned.
