THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY MAY 211 1881. WARRINGTON POLICE CASES. MONDAY.—Before Major Cartwright (Chairman), Alderman Burgess, and Couucillor Fairclough. MAJOR CARTWRIGHT AND THE MILITIA--Major Cart- wright said before they commenced the business of the Court, he was going to ask the magistrates to allow him to make a few observations with regard to what transpired at the Court en Tuesday last. The other magistrates each signified their willingness to allow Major Cartwright to speak. He then said; I would like to ask the Clerk a question. It appears from a report in the papers, of which I have been totally ignorant of until Saturday night, that there has been a letter written by the Mayor, and it is dated from the magistrates' clerk's office; I ask respectfully, Mr. Clerk, is that an official letter ?—The Clerk: Oh, yes.— Major Cartwright: Drawn up by whom?—The Clerk; Written by the Mayor; drawn up at his request by me. It is an official letter from him to Colonel Mansergh.—Major Cartwright: It didn't suggest itself to you at the time that it would have been more courteous towards me to have given me some information about tke accusation 2—The Clerk: There is no accusation against you. Your name was only mentioned as a magistrate.—Major Cartwright:l Oh, but you must have given him NM information. Didn't you think that out of courtesy to me you, as adviser hf the Mayer, should have suggested that this should have , been referred to me, being the party attacked 2—The Clerk I didn't understand that there was any attack at all in the matter.—Major Cartwright; I think I shall be able to show that there has been something of the sort, inasmuch as the letter in the Liverpool Echo appears very differently, be- cause as you know, and every member of this Bench knows, that the Mayor is not responsible for any remarks that I make at this Bench. lam the re- sponsible party. This official letter is written in a very singular sort of way. It says simply that because I was not in the chair, although entitled to it, that it only emanated from an individual magistrate, and that is as much as to say it is not worth noticing. If Colonel Mansergh had had the courtesy when he knew my name, and I am no stranger to him, to have written to me for an explanation, I should have been quite prepared to have given it him in full. I flatter myself that I am quite capable of defending any charge that the gallant Colonel may have against me. He says herein a letter to the Echo and I am sorry I did not see it before this time or I should Echo, made some observations earlier :—"Sir,—With reference to a paragraph in your issue of the 10th inst., reporting a speech made by a magistrate of the borough of Warrington reflecting on the character of the Militia now quartered in this town, I have the honour to request you will be good enough to publish the enclosed copy of a letter received from the Mayor of Warrington, showing that the magistrate made a most unwarrantable attack on the character of the men of the regiment under my command.—l have the honour to be, sir, your obedient ser- vant, JOHN S. MANSERGH, Colonel,Commanding 4th Royal Lancashire Militia. Warrington, 12th May, 1881." I &ty I , made no unwarrantable attack on the men. What I said was with regard to the man that was brought up before us, and I venture to say that the court will agree with me that the remarks that fell from me were well deserved. I have been unable to see the report in the Echo of last Tuesday, and therefore I am making a statement in the dark as far as regards that report, but I have looked over the re- port of The Examiner and the other papers we have, and I don't find anything in those reports that anyone can take exception to. The case that was Nought before us on Tuesday was a case that if Col. Mansergh had had the whole of the evidence placed before him he would, as a sensible man, have come to the conclusion that my action in the matter was right and just. It is all very well for Colonel Mansergh to be as desirous as possible that the men under his command should conduct themselves in a proper manner, and lam anxious, very anxious that that should be so. He will find, and others will find, from last week's report that the Mayor hada case before him on Monday, we on Tuesday had a case before us, and the magistretes on Wednesday had also a bad case before them. In the latter case the man had made use of most disgusting language, and Alderman Davies remarked that it wae a bad case and ought to be punished. Now, I say that unless we do punish these men as they deserve when they are brought before us we shall have repetitions of this sort of thing, and so long as I am upon this Bench and have such fellows come before us as that one the other day, I shall be the first to meet the matter with the punishment it deserves. These men are not satisfied with creating disturbances in the neighbeurhood, but in many instances they hinder our officers in the execution of their duty, and I am sure I have heard the chief- constable say that they have given the police officers a vast amount of trouble. I don't consider I have been fairly treated in this matter, seeing that this correspondence has been going on without giving me any notice whatever—the person most interested in it. I thank you, gentlemen, for giving me an opportunity of making the statement I have, but I felt in duty bound to nuke it. I don't charge the men with anything. Those I have to deal with are those that are brought before me here; I have nothing to do with them more than that, and it is this case alone that I com- mented upon. I made no unwarrantable attack against the regiment under the command of Colonel Mansergh. I should be very sorry to do so.—The ordinary business of the court was then proceeded with. ,A CARELESS CARTER.—Hugh ardley, a carter, was charged with obstructing the footpath at Bridge Foot, on the 12th instant, by driving a horse and cart over the foot- path, doing damage to the amount of 6d. A man named Donnelly said that the defendant's lurry narrowly escaped running over his feet —Defendant pleaded guilty, and he was fined ss. and costs. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES.—AIice Henshaw, a widow, was summoned for not sending her daughter Sarah regularly to school.—Mr. Riley said the defendant bad had the school 'fees paid by the Board of Guardians since 1879, and the attendance had been very bad, having only been present at school 44 times out of a possible 290. Defendant was fined ss.—Patrick Roach was charged with not sending his son to school. Mr. Riley said this was defendant's seventh appearance for this offence. The boy had only made 32 out of a possible 440 attendances, and he could neither read nor write. Mr. Riley suggested that the boy be sent to an industrial school.—The Bench made an order for his com- mittal to an industrial school until he was 16 years of age. —Mary Cane was summoned for a similar offence.—Mr. Riley remarked that this was the defendant's fourth offence. 'lire boy, although 121 years of age, could neither read nor write. It was a most aggravated case.—The Beneli ordered the boy to be sent to an industrial school —Francis Males was summoned for not sending his son William to school, and he was fined 55.—William Hacking was charged with not sending his four childrek reeularly to school.—Mr. Riley said it was a most troublesome case, and the boys ineteed of I going to school were constantly playing about the streets.— Mrs.Hackingisaid William. who was 13 years of age bad run away about nine days ago, and km wished him to be sent to an industrial school. About November he ran away from looms and staved for some time, anti when he returned he was covered with sores. Through his aesociat- hog with the other children they all contracted the disease, mid were unable to attend school 'I hey load up to that time attended school regularly.—Mr. Riley said the attend- ance of the children for the last fifteen months hael been vet), irregular.—Mr. Hunt said the woman had seoken to him several times about the conduct of her boy William. He was perfectly incorrigible. William was ordered to be sent to an industrial school, and a fine of 5s was imposed in etch of the other cases.—For not sending his son Thomas to school. Thomas Rouse was fined ss. Alessns. JOLLY AND CO. AND THEIR WORE/SEN.—Petrick Ford was summoned for not sending his children regularly te school.—Mr. Riley observed that the boy had only made .42 attendances out of a possible 440, and the only excuse the parents made when either he or his assistant called was that they could not spare him and his mother was poorly. Mr. Riley, to show that the case was not one of poverty, handed to the Bench a note from defendant's employers, Messrs. Jolly and Co., file cutters, stating that defendant's weekly earnings were 30s.—Defendant's wife, who ap- peared, said that was not to, as he bad to pay ss. a week for jewellery. In answer to the Bench, she said tloe men were compelled to take the jewellery or be "sacked." Her hus- band had had to pay 21 for three watches, and to get them off ' his hands had been obliged to sell them for £9.—Mr. Riley: Really, gentlemen, do you believe any such tale that the man is forced to buy watches and sell them at such A reduc- tion ?—The Bench considered there was no doubt of the defendant's neglect, and imposed a tine of ss. in the cese of each child.

DESERTER.—Frank Minton and Thomas Connor were I charged with being deserters from the 22nd Regiment , stationed at Chester.—Prisoners pleaded guilty, and they were remanded to Walton gaol awaiting an escort. PFTCR AND Tose.—Patrick Burke, a boy, was charged , with playing at pitch and toss in Shuttle-street on the pre- ! vious day.—Defendant bad is. 4d. in his possession, and his mother in explaining this, stated that it was what the boy , had saved to get his clothes eut of pawn so that he coulu joirrtbe scholirs on walking-day. She had pawned his , clothes.—The Bench said a stop must ,he put to gaming, and fined the defendant 2s. In ROBBERY FROM A Comma HOLISM—Sarah Ann Jackson, a young woman, of no settled abode, was charged with stealing from the lodging him's° of Edward Mallarkey, King-street, on Sunday, a black serge jacket, value £1 es., a shawl 10s., and a purse containing 33.811.—h appeared prisoner anrived in town from Widnes on Saturday with a man named Antrobus, a native of Runcorn, and lodged at the house in question as man and wife. The woman stayed in the house the whole of the day, but towards night went out, and shortly after her departure a lodger discovered the robbery. Information was given to the police, and the prisoner was apprehended at Sankey Bridges by P.C. Whit- , tinghatn. She WEB wearing the shall, and carrying the jacket under her arm.---Prisoner pleaded guilty and she was committed to prison for three nionths with hard labour. CHIMNEY ON Fnua—For this offence, on the 10th inst:, doseph Parks was fined Is. TUESDAY.—Before Major Cartwright (chairman), Alderman Webster, and Councillor Fairclougb. ASSAULT ON A WOMAN. Patrick and Catherine Hennessy, father and daughter, were charged with assault- ing Margaret, wife of John Manion, Hying at Cropper's- brow. On Saturday night about half-past six, a militiaman named Cunningham, insulted the prosecutrix, and imme- diately afterwards the prisoners came on the scene, made use of very bad language, and struck the prosectatrix on the face. Prisoner Catherine sent a stone into prosecutrix's house, which broke a mirror on the mantelpiece. Presecu- trix sent for a picket, but they took no action in the matter, and about nine o'clock, when prosecutrix was going to the market, the prisoner Catherine followed her down a yard, and she was compelled to go into a house for protection. A large number of witaesses were called for both prosecution

and defence, and there was a great amount of conflicting evidence.—The Bench characterised the evidence for the defence as disgraceful, and said there was no deubt the pro- secutrix had been badly treated.—The male prisoner was discharged, and Catherine was bound over to keep the peace for six months, herself in £lO, and two sureties in £5 each.
WEDNZSDAY.—Before Alderman Davies and Councillor Fairclongh.

REFRACTORY TRAMPS AT THE WORKHOUSE. -- Thos. Brown, John Cox, James Mathie, William Harrison, and John Meacock, vagrants, were charged that they, being in- mates of the casual ward of the Warrington workhouse, on Tuesday, did unlawfully refuse to perform the task of work set them by the master. It appeared that prisoners worked outside at their task from about six o'clock until eight o'clock on Tuesday morning, and the rain, which had been falling during almost the whole of the time, began to fall very heavily, and they went into what is called the big room to shelter. They stayed there over two hours, and ' then the remainder of the stones they had to break were brought in, but they refused to break them. One of the prisoners stated that there was no fire by which they could dry their clothes, and that they were all shivering through being in their wet clothes. They would not have refused to have done the work inside at first, but it was eleven o'clock —the time at which they should have gone out—when they were asked to do it inside.—Curry, the porter at the work- house, admitted there was no fire on that 'morning, but there was a stove in which they could dry their clothes at night. —Maguire Ward, who said he was foreman over the out- workers at the Workhouse, and was an inmate of the House because he was subject to rheumatic, said the prisoners went inside immediately it commenced to rain. The Bench ex- perienced some difficulty in eliciting from witness that the men were locked in the room, which caused Alderman

Da-vies to remark that the "rheumatic man;;d-Curry had given their evidence in a "rheumatic fashion."—Curry, in answer to Councillor Fairclough, said the men had each 3 cwt. of stones to break, and if the men had finished that task

in half an hour they were then at liberty to go, but they must break that quantity unless through weakness they were unable to do so.—Prisoner Brown said he bad not 20Ibs. of his stones to break when they went inside, and the others said the same. —Alderman Davies thought the porter might have considered the inclemency of the weather before ha sent the men outside.—Ward said he wore his clothes all the day.—Alderman Davies : You have the theumatic. (Ltughter.)—Mr. Hunt said the prisoners had . . . .

, been locked up since th,e previous morning, and they had behaved very well.—Alderman Davies: But you have no I stones? (Laughter.) Mr. Hunt: Only what they walked on, sir. (Laughter.)—Mr. White: They have not broken those, have they? Mr. Hunt: No, sir.—Alderman Davies said he and his brother magistrate, considering that the men had only a small quantity of stones to break, and that they got wet, should discharge the prisoners. He was very loth to let men off in that fashion, but he was inclined to think _
they had bad sufficient punishment it any punishment was required.—The prisoners: Thank you, sir.

THIIRSDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds, and E. Milner, Esq. FALSE ENLISTMENT.—James O'Neil, alias James Gray, a native of Runcorn, was charged with making a false answer on attestation before a magistrate during enlistment for service on the 10th inst., at the 13th and 14th Brigade Depot. —From the evidence of Provost Sergeant Cam- bridge it seemed the prisozer enlisted on the 10th inst. and was passed by the surgeon major as fit for service, but it had since been discovered that the prisoner had been discharged from the 10th Huzzars as lunatic.—The Bench committed him for 14 days' hard labour.

FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds and Messrs. Z. Armitage and John White. DEFAULTING FUSTIAN CUTTERS.—Bridget Higgins, a fustian cutter, was summoned to show cause why she should not be committed to prison for disobeying an order of the magistrates requiring her to fulfil her contract with Mrs. AsPeY. She had been committed several times for the same offence, but she promised to at once go to her work, and the case was adjourned for a week.—lane Riley was simi- larly summoned for not fulfilling her contract. She was committed to prison for 14 days.—Mary Mockan and Matilda Carlisle for like offences, were committed fora similar period. John Dagnall was summoned for £2 15s. damages by Mr. Platt, having been away from his employment since Feb- ruary 24th. As defend int had attended his work daring the week, Mr. Platt said he would not press the case, but ask for ss. and costs. The Bench made the order at the rate of is. per week.—Orders were made on Annie Clark, Mary Ann Joyce, Bridget Mea, Mary Tivenan, and William rown, to fulfil their contracts with Mr. Platt, and pay damages and costs.

CHARGE Acumsr A PunucAw.—lienry Budge, landlord of the Eagle and Child public-house, Bridge-street, Warring- son, was summoned for allowing liquors to be consumed on his premises during prohibited hours, and F. Massey, F. Wall,JohnLongshaw, and John and Rd. Warburton were summoned for being found on the premises. Mr. kludge pleaded guilty to allowing the beer to be consumed, but not to selling it.—P.S. Spinks said that on: Tuesday morning at ten minutes to one he was passing up Bridge- street when he noticed a light. On entering defendant's parlour he heard somebody order drinks, and saw Mr. Budge pass towards the bar, heard him draw the drinks, and take them in to where the men were. He then entered that room and discovered the whole of the defendants, seated very comfortably round a table, with the liquor before them. —Captain Reynolds: They would not be very comfortable when they saw you. (Lauater.)—Witness said he asked Mr. Budge if he had a special license, but he got no answer, nor any explanation. The other defendants said that Mersts. John and Richard Warburton, of Grappenhall, had called there on their way to Newton fair, and a horse they bad with them bad become dangerously ill. They were in consequence obliged to put up at the house, and they had been waiting for Mr. Wall, who !tau just arrived, and was doctoring the horse when witness toads his appearance. He saw the horse, and it appeared very M.—Defendants made a statement which agreed with that of the ofacer.—Mr. Hunt said Mr. Budge had occupied the house since April, 1878, and he had nothing whatever against him. He regarded bin as a very respectable man. —The Bench considered there had been no wish to break the law; that the offence had been committed uninten- tionally, and the costs would be imposed in each case.

The house is situated in a low locality, which is now being cleared as part of the condemned area.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-WEDNESDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-WEDNESDAY.

MR. BRADLAUGH: LANCASHIRE PETlTlONS.—Petitions were presented praying the House to admit Mr. Bradlaugh to take his seat, by Mr. Rylands from Burnley; against the Parliamentary Oaths Bill, by Lord Sandon from a public meeting in Hope Hall, Liverpool. EDUCATION IN SCOTLAND—Dr. CAMERON moved the second reading of the Free Education (Scotland) Bill. He 11 said the measure would only apply to Scotland, and its ob- ject was to enable the School Boards to pay the fees for children whose parents were unable to pay them from their own resources, without having, as was new required, to resort to the Board of Guardians, and thereby incur the reproach and stigma of being paupers.--after a long dis- cussion, the motion WES negatived without a division. NEW BILLS.—Mr. Bass brought in a bill to abolish the power of imprisonment for debt by inferior courts; ana Colonel Colthurst a bill to afford facilities for the obtaining of loans by the managers of industrial and reformatory schools in Ireland.

div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.—TuuRsDey.

THE RIGHT OF ASYLITM.—Lord LAMINGTON aSked whether the report was true that certain foreign powers had made representations to the Government respecting the right of asylum for political offenders in this country.— Earl GRANVILLE said the question had been raised frequently, but the feeling of this country on the subject was 80 very well known that he did not think such representations would be made. What had taken place was that Russia, with the consent of Germany, had applied to this country to join in a conference to consider what practical measures might be adopted in order to suppress the criminal machinations of certain associations, but Her Majesty's Government, even after thefrightful murder of the late Czar, did not think it right to join such a conference, not from any sympathy with I Nihilism, but because they thought that no practical results would be obtained from it.

div.head: LONDON CORRESPONDENCE.
div.p: LONDON CORRESPONDENCE.

On Monday night Mr. Gladstone delivered a speech which has perhaps created more sensation even than that with which he introduced the Land Bill. His appearance at the table was of itself a surprise, it having been arranged that the Solicitor-General for Ireland should on Monday resume the debate; but, as the Premier explained, he was not in a. condition of health to remain in the House till a late hour, and, feeling the necessity of speaking last night, he had dis- placed his colleague. This reference to the state of his health drew forth a general exhibition of sympathy. But it must be said that had the fact not been mentioned on this authority it would scarcely have occurred to anyone who heard the speech. The Premier brought with him to the table the stick which has formed his constant companion since the night the House met after the Easter recess. Leaning on this, he delivered the opening sentences of his speech; but as he warmed to his work, the stick became rather a burden than an assistance, and presently :it was laid upon the table, and he stood upright, eking out his speech with all those ges- tures which mark his delivery on occasions when he is deeply moved. It was towards the end that he burst upon the House with what some will call a menace and others will regard as a warning. Mr. Gladstone spoke for an hour and a half, and when he sat down, in prolonged cheering from the Liberals, he left the Bill n about as clear a position as ever a Govern- ment measure was placed. Several things are now beyond question—first, what is scarcely new, the Ministry will stand or fall by the Bill; secondly, they mean to have the i Bill in all vital respects such as it stands now, yielding neither to the Irish members on the one side no; 'the Con- servatives on the other. Mr. Gladstone acknowledges the necessity of preparing for the ordeal of passing it through the Lords, to which end his speech last night will doubtless materially contribute. It was designed for the benefit of and addressed chiefly to the Conservatives. It was listened to with profound attention by a large number of peers who crowded the gallery. In all political circles within the House it has created a profound sensation.

Mr. Gladstone was very much worn out by his efforts last night. He did not speak long, but he threw more than usual energy into his speech. Whilst the glow of oratory was upon him he was equal to the task. The relapse has proved unusually severe. If Mr. Bradlaugh is made a bankrupt, it will be for no mean sum. It came out in court to-day, that he is sued for
no.less amount than £355,500. His Original intention was

to have £50,000 worth of voting, but like many other people who indulge in luxuries, he would seem at leak to have entered upon a reckless extravagance with regard to division, and to have gone into more lobbies than a wise economy would have approved. It is said that the Attorney- General can release him of his liabilities, but this, I believe, is a mistake. Sir Henry James may remit the penalty due to the State, but cannot limit the money which should go to the common informer. The said common informer, "if" he recovers the money, will be able to retire from his profession and go to court. One almost regrets that there are not more Bradlaughs, that there might be more penalties.

There is no doubt that the anxiety and worry of public business are telling seriously on Mr. Gladstone's strength. He is one of the last men to complain without good cause ; and when he referred on Monday at the beginning of his speech to the bodily weakness which rendered it necessary for him to leave the House at an early hour, he conveyed to his audience but a faint idea of the illness from which he was really suffering. Hi a intense earnestness, and his sense of the grave importance of the subject, supported him throughout his speech, but at the end the right hon. gentle- man was evidently exhausted, and went home at once to bed, from which he had not risen on Tuesday. There is no doubt that the Premier must be persuaded to take as little share as possible in the discussion en the Land Bill when that measure gets into Committee, and I hear that the strongest representations have been made to him by his col- leagues, who urge that there is no necessity for the right hon. gentleman to conduct the bill through the committee stage, the management of which may well be left to Lord Hartington and Mr. Forster. I have reason to believe that the statement that Prince

eopold is about to be made a Royal duke, with the title of Duke of Albany, is correct. That he will sooner or later I receive that distinction may, of course, be taken for granted. Prince Leopold is the only one of the four Royal brothers who has not a seat in the House of Lords. Yet by intellec- tual training and personal inclination he is the most fitted to to take his place in the Senate. The time assigned by rumour as that chosen by Her Majesty for conferring a dukedom upon His Royal Highness, and the title which it is said has been chosen to illustrate the dignity, are both of them fitting in the circumstances.

F All persons have heard of travellers in American "notions;', the Prince of Wales is a traveller in Ebglish notions. Now he travels in smiles and new in tears. One week he sets forth to the Russian capital to prove to its inhabitants how fine a stock of sympathetic mourning is kept always on hand in these islands; the next he starts off for the gay metropolis of Austria with a choice selection of jocund say- ings and a countenance expressive of radiant happiness. Between the fulfilment of these two commissions he has! executed several little jobs of .an analogous character at home. He has paid his tribute to departed greatness in an English churchyard, and a day or two later has produced his best specimens of beamingly sympathetic gladness on the occasion of a nuptial ceremony in an ancient shrine. But his business and its associations have systematically accompanied him; and whenever he has shown himself he has been forcibly reminded by facts that, whatever he may be in the future, he is at the present the travelling agent of the great House of Hanover and Guelph.

SUICIDE AT KNOWSLEY. -On Thursday, a farm labourer, named Henry Owen, 59 years of age, died in the Prescot Union Workhouse Hospital, whither he had been removed, in consequence of having cut his throat at Knowsley, on the 29th April. Deceased, who was employed on the farm of Mr. Robinson, had been suffering acutely from bronchitis and had had a quarrel with a woman, and on the night of the 28th ult., he retired to bed in a some- what disturbed state of mind. On the following morning, as he did not put in an appearance, search was made, and he was found lying in bed with his throat cut, and the bed clothing saturated with blood. Dr. Hall, of Prescot, was sent for for and he attended and stitched up the wound, and ordered the nd man to be removed to the Workhouse Hospital, where he expired as above stated.

_ PEIMITIVE METHODIST BAND OF HOPE, ST. HELENS.— On Monday a special entertainment in connection with the above Band of Hope was given in the School-room, Kirk- land-street, to a good audience. The first part of the pro- gramme consisted of recitations, which were rendered by Mr. J. C. Westworth, Miss Wells, Mr. John Lawrenson, Miss Lindon, Mr. Charles Hodgetts, and Master Albert Lucas; and songs by Mrs. Mellor, Mr. Skaife, and Mr. Wright. All were well given, and seemed to be enjoyed by the audience. Mrs. Wright acted efficiently as accompanist. Mr. J. B. Leach presided, and having to leave at nine o'clock he called upon Mr. IL Greenall to take his place. Mr. Leach, in a brief address, impressed upon the Band of Hope members the necessity of keeping their pledge. He was glad to see such a good meeting; the programme had, so far as he had heard, been excellent, and reflected great credit upon the gentleman who had the trouble of getting it up. He was sorry he had to leave, as he would have been pleased to hear the next part of the programme; but as he had indisposition at home, Mr. Prescott, the secretary, had promised to let him go.--The next part of the programme consisted of an amusing and instructive sketch, "Wanted, a confidential clerk." The .o.loning were the characters: Jonathan Dobbs, in want of a confidential clerk, Mr. J. C. Westworth; John McCormick, a servant in the employment of Dobbs, Mr. James Williams ; Horatio Lushirgton, fond et beer, Mr. Robert Mustard; Charles Valentine, who is very im- portant, Mr. John Lawrenson ; Dick Sharp, who thinks he knows a thing or two, Mr. R. M. Prescott; Harry Dalton, successful applicant, Mr. R. Foulkes. The parts were well taken, Mr. Westworth making an excellent principal, and he certainly exhibited a partiality for proverbs. His servant made a first-rate Irishman, and seemed a favourite with the audience. In the applicants the first to be noticed was Mr. Robert Mustard, who performed his part well, and his style brought roars from the audience. Dick Sharp was well taken by Mr. Prescott, and he had the audience convulsed with laughter at the manner in which he took tbe principal off. Mr. Foulkes was particularly suited for the character of Harry Dalton. The sketch was a complete success, re- flecting credit on all taking part. After this the meeting was brought to a close.—Cona.

BOLD-STREET CHAPEL, WARRINGTON.—T chapel, which has been closed for a short time, has been thoroughly beautified and renovated, and will be re-opened to-morrow (Sunday), when special sermons will be preached. CHURCH OF ENGLAND BONE Miioses. —On Sunday, the annual sermons in connection with the Additional Curates' Aid Society, were preached at the Parish Church Runcorn; in the morning by the Rev. C. P. Milner, M.A. and in the evening by the Rev. Canon Barclay. The collec- tions amounted to £l2 124.

MAD BULL AT PRESCOT : NARROW ESCAPE OF A Boy. —On Monday afternoon, while a young bull, belonging to Mr. Critchley, butcher, of Rainhill, was being driven through Present, it became excited, and dashed into the garden and yard of Mr. Thomas Lyon, mineral water manu- facturer, Warrington-road, upsetting 0. number of boxes of patent bottles, and otherwise doing damage. The animal hadtno sooner been got out than it made another attempt to obtain admittance to the garden, but this time it was roughly repelled. The boll then dashed across the road into Derby- square, where it continued to carry ou its pranks for two or three minutes, running and kicking at anything that impeded its progress. Shortly afterwards a number of boys gathered on the road with the intention of preventing its going back into the town, but it dashed at them, and one of the boys named Roby, residing with his parents at East- view, had a narrow escape of being "(upped," Just as the animal was on the point of striking Lim with its horns, he slipped and fell in front, and it gassed directly over,without, fortunately, in the least injuring him. There is not the least doubt that if he had not fallen at that moment he would have been tossed, and the consequences might have teen serious. The bull proceeded at a rather quick pace along Warrington-road, charging at everyone who en- deavoured to check its mad course. After much trouble the animal was at last got to go safely to its destination.

THE FATE OF A Sr. HELENS Yorrx.—ln looking over the list of the lost in the ill-feted ship, Doterel, we find recorded the name of Henry Myers, Ist class, boy, son of My. Wm. Myers, of Liverpool-road, in this town. He had, pre- viously to entering the navy, been connected with the St. Thomas's Church and school, and on Sunday morning last the vicar, the Rev. J. C. Pigot, in his sermon, referred specially to his loss. He took for his text the passage of scripture "Watch, therefore, for ye knew not what hour the Lord doth come." In an impressive set mon the rev, gentle- man implored his hearers to be most earnest in their work ; and referring to the loss of the Doterel, said that that terrible circumstance was brought home to them more forcibly by the fact that the young seaman, Myers, who was one of their owp, was on board at the time of the accident, and perished when doing his duty. He spoke in high terms of his cisaracter, and seemed much affected throughout the sermon. The parents and relatives of the deceased youth were present, and special and appal p late hymns were rendered by the choir. We may say that Myers had only been two years in the navy, and that this would have been his first -voyage. He had for 18 months previously been on H.M. training ship Impreguable, and only sailed with the Doterel on the 23rd December last. He bore an excellent character from his officers, was ranked first-class, and had received three separate badges and a crown for good conduct, and a first-class certificate on account of his being a total abstainer. He was thoroughly conversant with his duties, having passed all his examinations, and was looked upon by the officers as a young seaman likely to make his way in the service. He was respected end liked by all on board, and numerous friends and relatives here now mourn his loss. We can only express our regret that such a clever and promising young sailor should have been taken from the service by such a terrible accident.

post of Minister of the Interior, vacated by General Blelikoff, can be viewed in no other light than that the new Czar has determined to inaugurate his rule by showing his subjects that he has the will as well as the power to govern by sheer force, and wlthoat any of those lighter and more endurable chains which link a sovereign and his people in bonds of amity and mutual respect. The Emperor and those who have assisted to fashion his policy, cannot, we are sure, flatter themselves that under the new regime they will do any more than keep the people in awe; but ruling by terror cannot prevail in these days of Constitntional Government. Many of those who revere the Czar will be driven into the arms of his avowed enemies, and those who might perhaps have been led into less anarchical paths by considerate and conciliatory treatment will harden their hearts at the intelligence that might, and not right, is to be the mainspring of the Czar's Government of his subjects. That Nihilism will not be overawed by force, however terrible, the history of the past few years convinces us. It is, indeed, the fructifying influence under which it grows and spreads. Violence will be met by violence, and terrorism by terrorism. In their recent pro- clamation, in reply to the Emperor's manifesto, these revolutionaries say: "We accept the war forced upon us by your Majesty. We shall persevere, and are .confident to achieve victory; the greater the oppression the firmer will the people become, and if one of us is killed, there are ten eager to take his place. We have not hitherto been afraid of your powder, nor shall we be in future." This certainly does not look like being overawed by the despotic power of the new Czar and bodes ill for the future. While social and domestic reforms in the gigantic Russian Empire are thus pushed on one side with a disdainful band, it is some consolation to know that there are signs that the new Czar is anxious to abandon much that is cumbrous and useless in gm military system which has existed in the time of his predecessors. A scheme embodying a number of re- forms in thi3 direction, will, it is stated, be submitted shortly to the Council of.Scate, which looks remarkably well on paper, but we fear that there is too much reason to believe that officialism and red tape will strangle even these much needed reforms in their birth.

The Runcorn Burial B )ard had before them, at their last meeting, the question of whether it was their duty to pay the bills for washing the surplices of the vicar of the parish, the Rev. Canon Barclay. The subject appears to have been introduced by the secretary, on presenting a bill from one Ann Ford, which included the sum of 3s. for washing the surplices. The secretary (Mr. Salkeld), seems to have been in a slight fog as to what the meaning of Mr. Glen really was, when speaking upon the provision of surplices, and other ecclesiastical matters, as he advised the Board that it was part of what was required of them in the carrying out of their important duties. Mr. Handley, however, sown put the opinion of Mr. Glen in its proper light, and showed clearly that the surplices ought to be provided by the parishioners in Easter vestry meet i ngassembled. Mr. Coleburn was quite of opinion that the Board had no power to pay any bill for providing either a surplice or a book containing the Burial Service. It was very wisely decided that in future no payment for washing surplices should be passed I may congratulate the ratepayers of Runcorn on the fact that the days of Church rates are gone for ever, 80 that if the parishioners at the Easter vestry meeting decide to pro- vide surplices, or to pay for the washing of them, they will have to do so out of their own pockets, in like manner as the believers in voluntaryism. And pray what hardship is there in such payment being made by the clergyman who makes such a splendid thing out of the fees ? Mr. Marshall asked if it would be wise to send a polite message to the vicar telling him to fctt his own surplices washed, and Mr. Littler had tht.. daring to propose that the clergy should get out of the difficulty by not wearing surplices! Fancy a minister of the Church as by law . established, without a surplice! He would be as wanting in authority as a judge without his wig, or his ermine. How Paul, the glorious apostle of the Gentiles—he before whom Felix trembled—managed to move all Asia Minor without a surplice, which he would probably have regarded as a relic of Judaism, is a perfect mystery to me !

The lovers of the fragrant weed, who are connected with the Runcorn branch of the Salvation Army, are having their devotedness put to a somewhat severe test at present. Captain Inman, who is in command at the Runcorn station, is stated to kave issued a sort of general order to the effect that the pernicious practice of smoking must be discontinued by every one of the members who holds an official position. I am informed that these instructions have caused no small amount of heartbutning and dissatisfaction amongst some of the members holding office, who look upon the captain as one who apparently takes pleasure in binding "heavy burdens "which are "grievous to be borne." I can hardly believe that the order has been issued by command of so shrewd a man as General Booth himself, though I must ad- mit that I have seen numerous condemnatory remarks as to smoking in the journal which specially represents the society. No doubt excessive smoking is injurious, but it must not be forgotten that some of the greatest men who have ever lived have been lovers of tobacco. I believe I am correct in saying that several of the most prominent ministers of the present day are great smokers, amongst whom I may instance the Rev. Hugh Stowell , Browne, of Liverpool. Several of the greatest men who have adorned English literature have smoked. Carlyle was a great devotee of the pipe, and as the wreaths of smoke curled up to the sky, as he sat in his garden, he was wont to pour forth those wonderful sentences which so impressed Ralph Waldo Emerson when he visited this country. I was much amused, some short time ago, in reading the life of Dr. Adam Clarke, the great commentator, to find how bitterly he often spoke against the use of tobacco in any shape; and, indeed, I believe that even at this day, there is a regulation to the effect that every candidate for ordination to the Wesleyan ministry has to be questioned as to whether he is guilty of smoking ! It seems that the captain of the Runcorn division of the Salvation Army, net satisfied with branding all dealers in intoxicating liquors as only fit to be consigned to eternal darkness, is determined to extinguish the tobacco dealers. Those who are successful in doing much good in the age in which they live, are seldom men of extreme views, but are generally willing to give other people credit for a little common sense as well as themselves, even though they are not inclined to pronounce their particular shibboleth. I hear that rather than submit to such tyranny, about a dozen of the officials have resigned their official rank, and that they intend to form a deputation for the purpose of consulting General Booth upon the question. The old adage," When the cat's away the mice will play," was exemplified in a very curious manner a few days ago. It is well known that depredations have lately been made upon fowl pens in certain localities, to the great annoyance of the peaceful inhabitants. A policeman residing in the burglar-infested district was lately on night duty, and there can be no doubt that, like an honest guardian, he zealously I discharged the duty entrusted to him of keeping a watchful eye upon his neighbours' property. My readers can, however, imagine the feelings which filled his bosom when, on return- ing to his own home in the morning, he found that his own fowls had been feloniously taken away. lam inclined to think that night duty in future will have an extra attrac- tion for this hapless officer of the law, as he will, of course, have a personal interest in the capture of the merciless culprits. More strangely than ever, though, must this in- cident impress us with the fact that When constabulary duty's to be done. The Policeman's lot is not a happy one." If there are any young gentlemen in this town who feel disposed to launch themselves on a clerical career, without due regard to its responsibilities, I would advise them very strongly to study well the report which has recently been presented to a meeting of the Corporation of the Sons of the Clergy. From this I learn that last year pecuniary assist- ance was voted to no less than 283 clergymen in distressed circumstances, while pensions and donations were given to 1,50 widows and aged daughters of clergymen, and apprentice fees, outfits, and educational grants were provided

The paterfamilias of lim:ted means will do well to reflect upon it before be advises his boy to enter the church for a living. He will see from the above that the Church of England, notwith- standing her enormous revenues, is unable, as at present constituted, to protect her ministers from the disagreeable realities of adverse fortune.

RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT WARRINGTON.—Under the presidency of Mr. J. Grounds, waywarden, a meeting of the ratepayers of the rural portion of the township of Warring- ton was held at the King and Queen Inn, Padgate, on Thursday night, for the purpose of authorising the way- warden to appoint a collector of the highway rate. It Was proposed and secotffied that the waywarden be authorised to appoint Mr. William Grounds as collector. This resolution not finding support, it was then resolved, with two dissen- tients, that the appointment of Mr. J. L. Tunstall, at the usual salary of £2O per annum, be sanctioned. A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the meeting. THE £4,000,000 FORTUNE.—A Bolton correspondent says he is informed from a source which adtnits of no doubt that the .£4,000,000 fortune has been abandoned by the expectant inheritants, on the ground of the hopelessness of establish- ing their claims. The difficulty which exists is not in John Seddon, of Bolton, proving his title to what was bequeathed to him by the late John Taylor, of Haslingden, but in the latter proving his own title to the property which formerly belonged to Sir Andrew Chadwick, who died intestate. Hitherto it has been impossible to prove who were Sir Andrew's heirs-at-law, though some time ago a number of persons in the locality of Bolton bearing the name of Chad- wick entered into a kind of family organisation with a view of taking steps for establishing their claims. BODY FOUND AT WIDNES. —Early on Thursday morning, a boy named John Rowles found the body of a I woman on a sand bank, near the Old Marsh. The deceased appeared to be between 45 and 50 years of age, she is 5 feet high, has dark hair (turning grey), is slenderly built, dressed in an old black dress, and nas on dark stockings with clogs, on which are new irons. The body is very much decomposed, and appears to have been in the water some weeks. It has been removed to the Cuminercial Hotel.

lAIINC/I OF A FIAT AT FENIIETII.—A flat intended for the river trade vias launched into the Mersey from the dock- yard of Messrs. Thomas Wilkinson, at Penketh, on Monday last. The launch was materially assisted by the high tide which prevailed, and the fore part of the vessel took the water almost as soon as she left the slips. The vessel was christened the Sprat, by Miss Johnson, of Penketh. This is the 15th vessel built by the firm at their yard at Penketh ; and they have named each of them after some kind of fish. The workmen and a number of friends adjourned to the Ferry Inn after the launch, and sat down to an excellent re- past, provided by Mr. Johnson.

COXING SERVICE OF SONG AT RUNCORN.—It will be seen from our advertising columns, that a service of song will be given in the Primitive Methodist school-room, Regent-street, on Monday evening, by the choir of Green- way-road chapel, in aid of their fund. The title of the service is " Christie's old organ," or " Honest Old Treffy and poor little Christie." The reader will be Mr. George S. Hazlehurst, and Mr. E. Billingsley will preside at.the organ. We hear that the choir have given the same piece in other places, with great success.

CATTLE DISEASE IN CHESIMIE.—The chief con stable of Cheshire (Captain Arrowsmith) has received reports that during the past week one beast had been atthked with foot-and-mouth-disease, one had died from that cause, and one had recovered. The disease had not appeared on any fresh farm during the week. The total number of animals attacked since the outbreak of the epi- demic is 472, of which one had been killed, ten had died, and 459 had recovered, there remaining two at present under treatment. No cases of pleuro-pneumonia or swine fever in the county are reported.

BREAKING INTO A WIDNES RAILWAY OFFICE.—DuT- ing Tuesday night an entrance was effected into the new offices of the Sheffield and Midland Co., at Moss Bank, Widnes, by breaking one of the windows and raising the latch. Two of the princip il drawers were broken open, and all the papers scattered upon the floor. An attempt had been made to break into a Miler's safe, which is kept on the premises, but it had not proved successful. On the clerks going to the place on Wednesday morning, and seeing the manner in which the premises had been ransacked, one of them, who usually kept his money in 1 one of the drawers, gave a chuckle to himself as he told his fellow workers that but for his having pod in 30s. on the previous night the thieves would undoubtedly have secured it. During the same day one of the company's detectives was busy making enquiries. A WIDNES CONCEET.—On Monday evening, & con- cert was given at Widnes, for the purpose of raising a fund for the help of James Dean, a workman who has been stricken with paralysis, and is entirely helpless, and has a Wife and four young children dependant upon him. Mr. Robert Shaw, of Runcorn presided. Mr. Grime and several other friends from Liverpool gave their services, as did also the excellent string band, led by Mr. Powell, and the several ladies and gentlemen who took part. The concert opened With the overture, "Caliph of Bagdad," which was well played, as was also Rosini's "Tancredi " in the second part of the programme. Miss H. Purver sung, in very good style, "Ruby," "Wishing cap," "Sights of London town," and "Half-mast high." Miss Laird gave "The skipper and hie boy" in a very pleasing manner. Mr. E. Thompson's singing of The death of Nelson" was well received, and he was greeted with an encore in "Empty is the cradle." I Miss Davies sang "The last chord" and "Three fishers," and Mr. Looney "The village blacksmith." Mr. Looney and Miss Laird were loudly applauded in the ! duet a What are the wild waves saying?" Mr. E. Grime's ' singing of "Within those sacred bowers," and "The skipper," were, without doubt, the gems of the evening, and were received with rapturous applause, and encored. The performances of the Widnes Temperance Hand-bell Ringers were given with effect, and encored. Mr. J. Glover, Mr. J. Tote, and Mr. Looney acted as accompanists. The pro- ceedings passed off very well, and much credit is due to the members of the Hope of Appleton Lodge of Good Templars, on whose suggestion the concert was got up. At the close, a very hearty vote of thanks was unanimously passed to those who had taken part, on the motion of Mr. A. Speak- man, seconded by Mr. T. Reay.
LATEST TELEGRAMS, &e..
THE PRESTON ELECTION.

The election of a parliamentary representative for the borough of Preston, in the room of the late E. Hermon, Esq., took place yesterday. Polling commenced at eight o'clock, and steadily proceeded up to noon, when there was a rush of workpeople to the various polling booths. The town during the day was visited by large numbers from surround- ing districts, and mach interest was manifested at the re- sult, party favours being worn by both young and old. Cabs and other vehicles were employed by both sides, and the feeling during the day was that Mr. Ercoyd would be re- turned. The poll was declared a few minutes to seven o'clock as follows :—Ercoyd, (3,004; Thompson, 4,340; majority for Ercoyd, 1,664: PROHIBITION OF OPEN-AIR PREACHING IN CALCUTTA. A telegram from Calcutta, yesterday, says :—The prohibi- tion of open-air preaching was decided upon by the munici- pal authorities in consequence of disturbances created by disorderly persons at such meetings. Under the terms of the municipal order none but duly licensed persons were hence- forward to be allowed to preach. The chairman of the mis- sionaries, however, refused to apply for licenses, claiming a prescriptive right uninterruptedly enjoyed by the mis- sionaries for years past. Last week, owing to fresh cases of disturbance, accompanied by assault, the Commissioner of Police issued a strict prohibition against all open-air preach- ing, and announced that any person disregarding the order would be prosecuted. The preaching, nevertheless, con- tinues, and the Commissioner of Police has consequently applied to the. Lieutenant-governor of Bengal for instruc- tions.

Another strike has taken place at Hossendale. The opera- tives employed by the Newchurch Spinning Company have struck work on account of alleged bad material. Negotia- tions are going on, and a settlement will no doubt be arrived at. The strike at Rairtenstall still continues. EXTENSIVE STRIKE OF SCOTCH STEEL-

div.head: WORKERS.
div.p: WORKERS.

The difference between employers and employed at Hillside Steel Works, Newton, :Scotland, has resulted in a I strike, the works having been stopped on Thursday night. The manager declined to be controlled by the men as to ther the steel should be made at Newton or at Blochairn, and, haying got the smelted steel wrought up, the wort were accordingly stopped. The strike is one of uno- large dimensions, as it affects 1,400 men. Should t extend to Blochairn, fully 3,000 men will be idle.• ms- pute arose on the question of making particular kinds of steel at Blochairn which had hitherto been manufacture] solely at Newton, and both masters and men are said to be determined to fight the point out. div.head: BILL.
div.p: BILL.

At the sitting of the committee yesterday, Sir S. Water- low, presiding, Sir E. Beckett, Q.C., the leading counsel for the River Weaver Trustees, addressed the committee on the evidence which has been laid before them. He contended that on all thezrounds on which the Bill was brought be- fore the House the promoters had failed to prove their case. Even supposing the subsidence was caused by pumping, he argued that the present law gave the promoters the protec- tion they sought for under the Bill, and asserted that a man bad a right to pump water even if it contained solids. He described the promoters as comparatively trumpery people, who, in order to increase their income, wished to kill the golden goose of Cheshire by imposing a ruinous tax on the salt trade.

General Gordon re-crossed the British frontier I will be seen from an advertisement in another column that a Ito-day. All well. Katmandu Nepal Maharaja died on the meeting in connection with the Farmers' Alliance will be 17th. The heir is placed on the throne. All is quiet held in the Co-operative Hall, on Wednesday next. The I hitherto. objects of the Alliance inclnde the securing of better repre- sentation of tenant farmers in Parliament, the stimulation of improved cultivation of the land, especially by obtaining security for the capital of tenants invested in the improve- ment of their holdings, the reform of laws relating to the ownership and transfer of land, the further reform of the game laws, the redemption of the land from the burden of extraordinary tithe charges, and the readjustment of ordinary tithes, dac. The chairman of the Alliance is Mr. James Howard, M.P.; the vice-chairmen, Messrs. James W. Barclay, M.P. and William Parsot s ; and I the trustees are Sir David Wedderburn, M.P. and Mr. W. Fowler, M.P. For many years it has been felt by those who understand the necessitiesof modern farming that the conditions under which the cultivation of the soil is carried on in Great Britain are highly detrimental to agricultural prosperity, being opposed to increased production, and, therefore, prejudicial to the interests, not only of landlords and tenants, but also of the whole community. The serious position in which tenants and landlords find themselves placed at the present time urgently demands that every legitimate offort be made to remove all impediments which stand in the way of the full development of the resources of the soil. The preliminary step in this direction must be to free the business of farming from the trammels of injurious laws, and ...the cultivation of the soil from the unwise and in many eases absurd restrictions which render its improvement difficult, if not impossible. The legislation of the past year, particularly upon the question of game, revived the languishing hopes of agricul- tural reformers. If the farmers of Great Britain desire to see similar and more important remedial measures brought forward and carried into effect, there ean be co doubt that they will have to put forth the most strenuous efforts, so as to convince Parliament and the country that they are in earnest. The surest step towards the removal of all agri- cultural obstructions which have to be dealt with by Pattie. ment is manifestly the election of men who really represent the interests of agriculture. The meeting bn Wednesday will be presided over by Mr. G. W. Latham, of Sandbach, and addressed by Mr. J. S. Leadam and Mr. E. Bear I (secretary) who will attend as a deputation. I The Chester Liberal Association has forwarded a I memorial to the Government on the recent report of the Bribery Commissioners. The memorialists dispute the state- ment of the Commissioners that 2,000 persons in Chester are open to some of the corrupt practices mentioned in the report, and they urge that, as there was "absolutely no buy- ing and selling of votes at the last election, and the corrup- tion was ef a most venial character," to disfranchise the city would be a grievous wrong. LIBERAL ASSOCIATION FOR WEST CIIESIHRE.—During the late election for West Cheshire the want of a Liberal Association was very keenly felt. The register was found to be in a most deplorable condition, a large number of electors, who had an undoubted right to be on, having been struck off at the instance of the Conservatives, the Liberals having been frequently unrepresented before the revising barrister. After the election, which it is well known proved ,ouch closer than was anticipated, a meeting of the Liberal i chairmen of districts was convened at Chester, and it was ii cided to form a county Liberal association, with its head- quarters in the county city. Mr. Robinson, of the Old Bank, Chester, has been appoiated honorary secretary, and notices 'v,re sent out on Saturday to all districts in the county i• questing them to convene meetings and appoint represen- wives to the county association, and to attenl to Uh? irganisation and registration matters at once. Meetings of Liberals for this purpose have been held at Nantwich and other places throughout the county during the week, the Liberals being determined to put the registration upon a Roper footing. Mr. Ernest Brasasey, solicitor, 44 Chester, is been appointed registration, agent for the Chester district.
CONFERENCE ON THRIFT.

A conference on thrift was held at the Mansion House, 1 yesterday, ender the presidency of the Lord Mayor. Lord Derby and Mr. Fawcett, who were expected, were not present. A resolution that for the better protection of the savings of the poor the law should prohibit the establishment in future of any friendly so- ciety without due actuarial certification of the sufficiency of its tables of contribution was proposed by Colonel Harcourt. seconded by Lord Lyming- ton, and supported by Mr. Sclater Booth and adopted. After considerable discussion on the advisability of interfer- ing by legislation with the arrangements of the working classes connected with friendly societies, the conference condemned legislative interference with their operation. ANOTHER DESTRUCTIVE FIRE.

A ffie took place at Skibbereen, last night, which caused the destruction of the Post Office, with its telegraph appara- tus, stamps, cte., and an adjoining bakery. Several persons amongst those who escaped from the Louses were injured and scorched by the flames.

TUNISIAN AFFAIRS. Further correspondence respecting the affairs of Tunis issued last evening contains despatches from March 23rd, 1881, to May 7th. On April 6th, in a despatch to Lord Granville, Lord Lyons states that M. Barthelemy St. Biller had that afternoon spoken to him of the operations in Tunis as if they were to be confined to the neighbourhood of the frontier, and to be directed only to the punishmmt of the lawless frontier tribes, but that he had reverted to the general grievances of France against Tunis, although he had repeated the assurances so often given that he considered that the annexation of Tunis to France would be a mistake and a misfortune. It was, however, he affirmed, absolutely necessary that French influence should be predominant in the regency, and that French enterprise should have fair play, and as a natural consequence take the lead. France could not allow any other Power to make Tunis the fulcrom of a lever with which to distarbthe French possessions in Africa. On April 7ta Lord GGranville,in a despatch to Lord Lyons, says he has had an interview with the French ambassador, and note of the assurance that there was no intention on the part of France to annex Tunas, and he hoped that while they obtained redress for the par- ticular incident they would not exaggerate in the i affair which might easily create. a certain amount of irritation n ether countries.

A thrum DROWNED AT Si'. HsraNs.—A. boy five years of age, son of Ann Topping, 77, Park-road, Parr, was found drowned in a clay pit, at Parr, at a quarter-past eleven en Monday night. Deceased was last seen by his mother , about seven o'clock the same evening. The boy was then in the house, and his mother told him to put his jacket on, or he would be catching cold. The boy went out, and not returning at nine o'clock she became alarmed, and causod enquiries to be made throughout the immediate neighbour- hood; but no tidings of the bay could be athered. Some men, amongst whom was James Stocks, of Park-road, collier, went with a light to a clay pit on some waste laud at the end of Johnson-street, Park-road, and near where the deceased lived- and after searching in the water found the deceased quite dead. It appears no one had sen deceased go in the direction of the I,it, which is at present very dangerous. The water is about sixteen feet from the top of the pit, the sides of which are nearly perpendicular. 'The pit is unprotected. There were no marks of violence on the body,

LETTER FROM THE FAR WEST. Dear sir,—Thinking perhaps a few lines from the Far West may be of value to you and your numerous readers, more especially as I perceive many of them are farmers, I will endeavour to give you a few particulars concerning our adopted country. We are natives of Liverpool, being in the carting line there also being well known to many of the farmers around Liverpool. Eight years this spring I left Liverpool with my family, and arrived here in Nebraska . with very little means but willing to labour. I took a home- stead of 80 acres of land which was all that a private man was allowed to do at that time, but now 160 can be taken by anyone. Then the red Indian was only a few miles away from us, but he was quiet; the Buffaloes ran wild also in and there. these parts, but I was tired of renting in England, fore I determined to get a home for myself and family. When we came here first, we had to go twenty miles for a iktle grocery, and forty miles with our grist. Then, hun- dreds of broad acres lay vacant,but now all is changed. A fine railroad runs close past my door, a town and railway station exists only one mile away, whereat produce may be t forwarded. We have a mail twice a day, mills close by, and all free lands are taken up. There is good land free out further west about 150 miles. All our schools are free, and we have good teachers and good schoolhouses. Every tax- payer has to pay a little for the support of the schools whether be has children or not. The climate is a little warmer in sammer, also a little colder in winter than in England. Our seasons are shorter, and things grow very sapidly. The soil is of a rich black colour, no stones, stumps, or clay. Some farms are well adapted for stock, others more for grain. Cattle do well here, also sheep. Wheat, rye, barley, oats, flax, and Indian corn, and all kinds of vegetation flourish here in abundance. We nave machinery of all kinds for the farm. A farmer can it down to plough whilst it is being drawn by three horses. All the grain and bay is cat by machinery. Then for the ladies we have sewing machines, washers, and also the great organ, if they need it, or the fine plum. Al Inost every farmers wife has a sewing machine. Now, Mr. Editor, I think if many of those farmers that are renting farms around you would come out here, they would do well. There are plenty of fine farms far around me, ranging from 10 to 12 dollars per acre, 160 acres in a farm, ethers 80, that is about £2 to £2 10s. per acre. Some of these farms have fine groves and all kinds of fruit trees. You may ask what makes them want to sell? Well, the American is always on the move, he is restless, and wanting to be rambling about. "Let us sell up and go out west," or "go back east." He is never long in one place, hut always think- ing be can do better somewhere else; while the Europeans are settled, and they will stick to their homesteads when 6TICO they have got them. Should any of your numerous readers wish to emigrate, this is just the place for them. Let them come and get homes of their own. I will send you any information you may need, and also help anyone with any experien:e here. If a few good farmers come and set up a cheese factory here, they would do well, for this is just the place where such is seeded. As regards fuel in Winter, we have coal, and plenty of it all the year. Should there be a strike amongst the colliers, as there has been here this year, we wait patiently until the masters and men settle it between themselves, and in the meantime we burn corn cobs, and corn stalks, and wood, so that we are never short -ef fuel.—Yeurs truly, JAMES SPENCER. Bethel Farm, Hampton Hamilton Co., Nebraska.

The St. Helens Town Council having applied to. the local Government Board for sanction to borrow £7OO for purposes of street improvement, Major Hector Tulloch held an inquiry into the matter on Thursday morning, at the Town Hall. There were present Aldermen Harrison (the rtyor) and Mcßryde ; Councillor Baxter, Messrs. Brewis (en clerk), Craik (deputy town clerk), Johnson (borough )reasurer), and P. McKinley. Mr. Brewis said that on examining the sketch no one would have eny difficulty in coming to the conclusion that the improvement was a most necessary one. The surveyor would give the particulars and estimate of the work, and the borough treasurer, if necessary, would inform them of the financiil position of the borough. Of course that had been so frequently before Major Tulloch that it was per- haps scarcely necessary to mention it. In answer to the Commissioner, Mr. Johnson said the rateable value of the borough was £222,191. Mr. Hart explained that the place of proposed improve- ment was Dark-lane, which they intended to'widen. The pr op er ty owners in that neighbourhood—Mr. Foster, Messrs. BOUTIIeS and Robinson, and Mr. Kurtz—had given up land tor the purpose Major Tulloch : You have made arrangements for the purchasing of the lands required for the improvement ? Mr. Bart : Yes. Major Tulloch : And there is no difficulty at all in re- spect to the land ? Mr. Hart: None, Sir. The bridge is a very small one, eleven feet wide, and that has to be widened. At the present time it is not possible for two vehicles to pass. Major Tulloch : Mast of the £7OO is for the land ? Mr. Hart: Yes, with the exception of £209 15s. 10d. Major Tulloch: Is there a great deal of traffic? Mr. Hart: There is a good d.al of traffic. Deputy Town CieTk: It is the only communication be- tween Sutton and Parr—two important manufacturing dis- tricts. Major Tulloch: Is the road paved? Mr. Hart: It is simply macadamised with slag. Major Tulloch: Does any of you gentlemen wish to say anything? You Mr. Mayor? The Mayor : I think it a most desirable improvement. It is very awkward at present being very narrow. It is rather isregnlar too, I think. Mr. Hart said it was 3 perfect bend, but the improvement when made would remedy that to a great extent. The Mayor: The gentlemen who have property in the zeighbourtiood are .‘bout to build stpon the land, or let it for buil din g purposes, so that tb - property would be in a line with the road, and that would be a great improvement. Mr. Mcßiotey : Are you goin.i: to level the brow, or keep It as it is. Making the brow less steep than it is, is just the thing that requil es to be done, so far as driving is con-

cerned. Mr. Hart wam undPrstood to say that that would necessi- tate an encroachment upon private property; but no doubt, in course of time, they would gradually lessen the incline. Mr. BaxtEr : It is the main thoroughfare in the township, and very much used. Major Tulloch : It seems a most desirable scheme on the

plan. Ur. Baxter: This ought to have been carried out some erne ago, but the Borough had got into difficulties, and round it neussary to be careful about spending money. Mr. McKinley: I think it would be a much more iesirable scheme if something- were to be taken off that

brow. Mr. Brewis : But we shall have to purchase the property. Mr. McKinley: But then it is weless to Mike such an improiement as is now contemplated. You ought to wake a good job of it. The Mayor : If we improve it by raising the road a foot, and taking off the breast of the brow, it would be better than it is. I notice an improvement since I used to ride over it formerly. It is not as steep as that called John Rill's-brow, and not as long. Mr. McKinley : It is not as long, but it is steeper. With the exception of the bridge and the approaches to the bridge, you can get two traps to pass anywhere. I have driven along there, and the greatest obstruction I have met with is the steam engine of Kurtes. Major Tulloch said that would be all he required, and the inquiry, closed.
