---- A C03111f011( OCCURRENCE: 'THIEVING BY WORKHOUSE I TEs.—Margaret Harris was charged with running away from the Union Workhouse, Whiston, with a suit of clothes value 215., the property of the Guardians.—Prisoner pleaded guilty the master, said the prisoner was an .—rtrheßwiC.l'lllorkellio' use, and on the 11th ult. she deserted, itnaTiantge woith her a suit of clothes.—The Clerk: What do you mean by deserted? Just explain to the magistrates how she went away.--Mr. Bicknell: On the 11th ult. prisoner, who was dressed in the workhouse clothes, was allowed a day out in order that she might visit her friends, but she failed to return. A policeman found her at St. Helens last night.—Mr. Earle: How long had she been in the work- house ?—Mr. Bicknell: She came in on the 27th August last year. it is a common occurrence for inmates to abscond with the clothing. There were no less than three cases that morning, and they were obliged to seek the assistance of the Bench in putting a stop to the practice.—The prisoner : I have all the clothes secure. I have not used them.—Mr. Earle. Where does she belong to? Mt. Bicknell: To St. Helens.—Mr. Earle: What brought her into the workhouse? Mr. Bicknell: She came into the workhouse suffering from disease.—Mr. Holt: What character did she bear in the workhouse ?—Mr. Bicknell : Well, we have strict rules in force, and she has not had an opportunity of showing her vicious propensities. A great deal of valuable property is constantly going in this fashion.—Prisoner was sentenced to fourteen days hard labour.—Ellen Hunt was charged with a similar offence.—Prisoner pleaded guilty to running awayl with the clothes, but denied that they were worth 215., as , they were "old hospital clothes."—The workhouse master stated that this prisoner absconded in September last, and they had great difficulty in discovering her in Widnes. She appeared to have made away with every article he took from the workhouse. Prisoner was only in the workhouse a few days, but she appeared to have been an inmate , frequently. She belonged to Widnes, and was well-known to the police, who have a long list of convictions against I her.—P.S. Bull said prisoner had been before the magistrates at Widnes no fewer than nineteen times. Committed to gaol for one month with hard labour.--Esther Williamson was also charged with running away with a suit of workhouse clothes. Pri- soner pleaded guilty.—Mr. Bicknell stated that prisoner , came into the workhouse on the 26th January, andabsconded with the clothing on the 16th March. Prisoner had pledged the clothing in Widnes. When she went she left a child in the house, which was still there. She was a regular work- house inmate, and was found in Widnes last night. Every article was marked with the Union stamp, so that the pawn- broker could not but have perceived it was Union clothing. He would see the pawnhtneen—Prisoner was sent to gaol for one month with haul labour, RIDING BICYCLES ON THE FOOTPATH: CHEEKY SWELLS. —Robert Warriner, clerk, was charged with riding his bicycle on the footpath in Damhouse-lane, Huyton, on the 29th ult.—The charge was proved by P.C. Hall, who stated that the defendant resided at Thornton Leigh, Huyton-lane. —Mr. Holt: Was there any reason why he rode on the footpath? Was the road bad? Witness: Yes ; there were some broken stones on the road.—Mr. Earle: Had he a bell ? Witness : No, eir.—Mr. Holt: Do you find this bicycle riding on the footpath a common occurrence in the neigh- -1 bourhood ? Witness: Yes, sir.—Mr. Earle: Were there any more there? Witness: There was another young fellow.— Mr. Earle: Has he been summoned before? P.S. Bull: No, sir. He is a respectable young fellow—A fine of 2s 6d and costs was imposed, the Chairman intimating that as riding bicycles on the footpaths WAS a common occurrence a heavier fine would be inflicted next time.—Robert Davies was charged with riding his bicycle on the footpath at the same time and place.—P.C. Hall said he caught hold of the defendant while riding his bicycle on the footpath. The defendant in the previous case was riding behind Davies, but he got away. leavies as'eed witness to look over the offence that time, and be would not do it again.—ln de- fence. Davies stated that the road was very bad, and at the time a horse and cart were coming along. The footpath was neither kerbed nor channelledp and, consequently. he did not think it was a footpath.—Mr. Earle said he knew the road very well, and there was a footpath.—Defendant further stated that it he and. his friend had not been "cheeky," the officer would have let them off. (Laughter.) —Defendant was ordered to pay is. and costs. COAL-STEALING AT WHISTON.—Mary Brattey was charged with stealing 60Ibs. of coal, value Id., from the Carrs Col- liery.—Joseph Storey, surface-foreman at the colliery, stated that on the 10th May he saw defendant picking coals off the bank at the colliery, and afterwards put them behind a hedge. She had about 6011 s. of coal in her possession. He ' charged her with the offence, and she asked to be forgiven' that time and would net do it again. The practice of steal- I ing coal had become so offensive that the proprietors had determined to take proceedings against offenders to stop it. He had previously cautioned ttie defendant, and others as well. A footpath ran close by the batik. It was abut four yards distant. There were no rails to protect the bank.— Defendant stated that women from Whiston and Prescot frequently took coals from the bank, and nothing was said to them.—Mr. Earle informed the defendant that as the police knew nothing about her she would only be fined ss. and costs, but if she Was brought up again for theft the fine would be very much heavier. The magistrates were of opinion that the colliery company should take steps to pro- tect the bank. If they would not do so they would always be exposed to the risk ot people taking coal.—Mr. Storey said the people were repeatedly warned and driven away, but as soon as his back was turned they came back again.— Mr. Earle said that if the company built a twelve toot wall between the bank and the footpath the people would not be there then. The company must protect their property.— Mr. Storey observed that the colliery proprietors were not in a position to erect a twelve-foot wall. THE HOLY SCHOOL, NEAR RAINHILL : IS IT EFFICIENT? —Joseph Strettle was sornmoaed at the instance of the Present Union School ettendance Committee, for failing to send his child, Samuel Strete le to school, on the 9.1 i May.— Defendant said his son Was Vory ill on that day.—Mr. H S. Welch, school attendance officer, said the child was not attending an efficient school. Those proceedings were taken, not so much to obtain e conviction against the parent, as to get an order for an inerfici int school, situated at the Holt, Rainhil I , to be closed—Mr. Spencely : Confine yourself to the charge against defendant—Mr. Welch said he visited the school at the Holt, which was kept by a man named Roberts, on the 9th May, but the defendant's son was not present. He had called upon the defendant several times, and the only excuse he made was OA as long as Mr. Robert's school was allowed to he open, so long would hie son be sent there. The question whether or not the said school was an efficient school for children to attend, might be settled by their worships. When he was at the school, no reason was given to him as to the boy's absence, nor was I anything said. about his being sick. The child Was nide years of age, and ought to he able to pass standard 2.—Mr. Earle: I am not aware that we have anything to do with the school.—Defendant handed the clerk a certificate from Dr. Morris.—Mr. Speneely stated that the certificate was datedl 16th May, and certifed that Samuel Strettle was suffering I from a-feverish cold. The certificate was issued seven days I subsequent to the time for which the defendant was charged.—Mr. Earle asked who was to decide as to whether the school Was efficient Or not.—Mr. Welch said their wor- ships could decide the question,—Mr. Earle would like to see the section of the Act giving- them nower.—Mr. Welch observed that when the children were brought before their worships they could examine them, end by that means judge whether or not the school waS efficient—Mr. Earle said be was not goinv to set himealf up as a schoolmaster. (Laughter.)—Ml. Welch said this practice was followed by the London magistrates.—ln anewer to Mr. Holt, Mr. Welch said it was a private school, and there were between 25 and 30 children attending it. No registers were kept. The school was simply like the Cave of Adullutn. There were efficient elementary schools within one mile of the defen- dant's residence. When he visited the Holt school none of children seemed to be having a really sound elementary education, and there Was no evidence that the children attended the school regularly—Defendant said he believed some of the best scholars going was turned out of this school. His son was delicate, and often under the doctor's care.— Mr. Earle thought the School Board ought to send some efficient officer to this school, who would be able to go into the box and tell them whether or not the school was an efficient one. He did not think the time of the court should be taken up in examinive children.—Mr. Spenceley asked Mr. Welch if he had any personal knowledge that the school was not efficient. Mr. Welch said Ile himself was a school- master, and he was quite prepared to say that the school was inefficient —Mr. Spencely : In what respect?—Mr. Welch: , In respect to the subjects taught. The children are taught ' to write in copy books, to read the Bible and Testament, and to do sums.—Mr. Welch wished, as the defendant's son was not present, that the case might be adjourned so that the boy could attend, but this course was not approved of, and after some further coneeleration, the next case was called, which was thet of Albert Lvon, who was charged with fail- ing to send his child, Thomas Loon, to school, on the 9th May.—The boy was present. —Mr. Welch said the boy in this case attended the same school at the Holt. He was nine years of age, and it was only fair to suppose that he would only he able to pass Standard 2. Children were not allowed to leave school until they had passed the fourth standard. To pass standard two a claild must be able to read, with intelligence, a short peragragh, write a sentence, read out, with pen end ink ; and in aritmetic to do addition, substraction, multiplication, and eimple division.—Having obtained the consent of the Bench, Mr. Welch put a few questions to the boy, all of ol'.ich, with one exception, he failed to answer. At the reeuest of Mr. ea eleh the boy wrote his name on a piece of paper, which was handed up to the Bench.—Mr. Welch said the magistrates would see what kind of teaching was carried on in this school, and under the circurnstences he thought their Worships would grant an order.—ln anewer h::, Mr. Earle, the defendant Strettle said the doctor saw his an about three times.—Mr. Earle said the Bench had &treed to dismiss the case againgt , Strettle, and Lyon weuld be areal ss. including costs.—Mr. Welch: Ido not ask for a lice. I ask for an order that the bey, in future, attend an efficient Public Elementary School. —The boy's mother site if her son was not to go to Roberts's school, he must go to Reinhill Natinnal School.—An order to that effect was accordingly made.—Mr. Welch intimated that proceedings weede he instituted O,Z iinst all the children going to the Holt School.—For failing to send their children to school. William 11,imall, Elizabeth Ed mird.l. James Johnston, e dward Forshew, and John Hughes wore fined 6d. and costs --James Soindish, VVlaiston, was sum- moned for not sending, hie chile, Elizabeth Standish to school, on the 12th May, but as it was shown that the officer had summoned the parent for the Wl'OD,., child, the case trees , dismissed. _

On Wednesday, a bazaar in aid of the Holy Cross Church was opened by Lord Braye, in the assembly room of the Town Hall, St. Helens. The substantial structure known as the Holy Cross Church, in Corporation-street, has been erected at considerable cost, but it has not yet been properly finished. It was decided some time ago to make an effort to raise funds for the purpose of erecting a wall and palisading round the church, and renovating the handsome windows, which have suffered materially from the vapours peculiar to a manufacturing town like St. Helens. The building is elaborately furnished, the most recent addition in the shape of gifts being a magnificent sanctuary lamp, which cost £l5O, placed over the new chancel arch, and a splendid tabernacle case erected upon the altar. About two months ago the members of the congregation with commendable zeal set about their task; and the fine and costly collection of articles exhibited in the Town Hall during the last few days ie the result of their labours. Near to the entrance door on the left was the Irish stall, over which were the words, " Erin-go-Bragh." This stall was superintended by Mrs. McKinley, Mrs. Donnelly, Mrs. Mooney, Mrs. Collins, Mrs. Curley, and several young ladies. The principal objects of interests were :—A figure of St. Patrick, to be raffled for; a bog-oak inkstand, worth £7, embellished with harp, runic cross, ancient round tower; musical boxes, pictures, drc. The adjoining stall of " The Children of Mary," connected with the Holy Cross and 1 Lowe House Churches contained some pretty bannerettes of costly material worked by the Sisters of the Good Shep- herd, at the Penitentiary in Glasgow. Three of these were valued at £l2, £ll, and £lO respectively, one of which was sold to Father Swift. A silver and iVery box was valued at £2. Amongst other things there were a beantiful Chinese cabinet, and a representation of Windleshaw Abbey, in the Olden Time, made of perforated canvass. Thie, stall was superintended by the Misses Swift, Appleton, Morris, Ash- ton, and Ashcroft. The Lowe House Stall was attended to by the Misses Grimshaw, Chisnall, Winstanley, Slater, and Johnson, and this also presented a number of costly and beautiful things to the view, amongst which we might men- tion a cab'net, with china, worth thirteen guineas; an In- dian 'cabinet, skilfully carved, and china models of the Cleopatra monolith. On the other side of the room, at the far end, stood the Omninm Gatherum Stall, over which the following ladies presided : The Missee Harrison, Wilson, Dunn, M. Coppul, E. Coppul, W. Wil- liams, Scott, Houlton, and Coleman. This stall bore a quantity of clothing of a varied character, chiefly for ladies. Mrs. Johnson's stall bad upon it a quantity of crewel work, tea cosies, antimacassars, &c.; a picture marked £lO lOs , "The shadow of the Cross ;" and two smaller pictures by Casaloni, one of them being a representation of Aloysiles at the point of death receivi,ng the sacrament. What was styled as Mrs. Grace's stall exhibited only a small collection of articles, but these wet% very valuable, and were chiefly sanctuary vestments and altar requisites. ' One set of vestments was worth £5O, and a chasuble was ' valued at £3O. A number of statues carved in wood were , priced at £6 each. This stall was attended to by Mrs. Grace; the Hon. Mrs. Clifford. Mrs. Beesley, Miss Maguire Miss Turner, and Miss Bradley. On Mrs. Latham's stall, pre- sided over by that lady, and Mrs. Fiddler, Mrs. Murray, Misses Tyrer (2), and Miss Middlehurst, there were articles of dress, walnut cabinet, musical box, Stc. The Holy Cross stall was presided over by Mrs. A. Dent-tett, Mrs. Chisnall, Mrs. Swift, Mrs. Birchall, Mrs. W. Middlehurst, Miss Mahoney, Miss Bellis, and Miss Brockbank. The original I humbug all was presided over by Mrs. Williams. The re- freshment stalls presented a pleasing appearance, and the viands mere of a varied description. The caterers were Mrs. Belli, Mrs. Ashton, and Mrs. Williams. As is usually the case at bazaars, entertainments of various sorts helped to swell the exchequer. Dancing behind the screen on the platform was indulged in freely by both sexes to the tones of a piano. The art of making fancy glass articles was plied energetically by a skilful woAman in one corner of the bazaar; and in the other corner anyone could revive 1 the pleasant excitement of a current of electricity for a mere nominal charge. The slight-of-hand performances by Pro- fessor Weber, of Liverpool, caused no little wonder ; and 1 his ventriloquial sketch, with automaton figures, provoked great merriment. His auditors showed their estimation of entertainment by repeated outbursts of applause. The art gallery, numbering 75 paintings, some of which were very costly, was well worth visiting, the charge of admission being threepence. The entire collection was on sale "at a considerable reduction." At three o'clock, Lord Braye, the ' newly-created Irish peer, opened the bazaar. On the plat- form, besides Lord Brays, there were the following gentle- men:—Rev. Fathers Ullatborne Cardwell, Fanning, De Haza, Henry Dignum, N.J., O'Neil, Swift, and DubberleY ; and Alderman Johnson. The Rev. Father CARDWELL said: I aria very glad to have the opportunity of introducing to you Lord Braye, who is a stranger to most of you. I know it is a fact that many of you have asked, who is Lord Braye? Why should ' babe asked te open a latzaar here? And whoever heard of him before? Well, there is a certain reason why we should have asked Lord Brays to come from London and to give up his duties there, in the House of Parliament, in order to come here and open this bazaar. A few years ago he stole from our neighbourhood that which he values more than all the beauteous things you see decorating this hall—namely, Lady Braye. (Loud applause.) Without any further words, I introduce Lord Braye to you, and he will now deliver his address. . Lord BRAYS then rose amid hearty applause, and said: I , have to thank Father Cardwell for the kind terms in which he has spoken of me. lam afraid my duties in Parliament are not so pressing as to prevent my sparing a little time to open this bazaar. I assure you I appreciate the honour the fathers have done me in askingme to perform this duty;, and I consider it an appropriate occasion on which to read the following address, which I have prepared When I first visited Lancashire some seven years since, I confess that I thought the atmosphere an oppressive one; there seemed to be nothing but smoke, fog, and unquiet. But after a better acquaintance with this illustrious county, I found that there was another atmosphere—an atmosphere of Catholicism which the rest of Englandteas never breathed for three centuries. Not only is the faith preserved in many of the towns, but even in the villages, in remote hamlets and hidden parishes. The village ill Little Crosby, near Liverpool, has been pointed out as the only entirely Catholic village in Great Britain, and I have ascerteined this to be the fact. Having accepted the honor which the Reverend Fathers who labor among you have so kindly done me in asking me to open this charitable meeting. I trust you will not think it out of place if, instead of confining my remarks to the particular object of this meeting, beyond indeed wish- ing it every possible success, which I most heartily do, I offer you a few remarks connected with our general prospects in this country. By the word our of course I mean Catholic Prospects, which are ours because they are dear to us all. How little are these alluded to in public, how little written about, how little talked about. You will perhaps think this a good sign, as indicating general peace and contentment, and a satisfactory state of thinge. But is it not also a sign of possible stagnation and want of zeal? Where a question is never ventilated. never dragged to a platform, the dignity of the eubject may be enhanced by silence, but its popu- larity wanes. We Catholics of England are a very small and insignificant body, and we should act like all small and compact bodies of men must act, if they hope for success, foot to foet and shmslder to shoulder. De we? Of course Ido not allude to our profession of faith, for if a person re- nounce one jet or tittle of those things which are "of faith," then and there that person ceases to he a Catholic. No ! we have had scarcely an apostate individual in the present generation ; the Catholics in England have held to their faith so nobly and firmly that I think even St. Paul, who praised the constancy of his converts in Rome. would if he were writing an Epistle now to tbn English catholiea praise them in like manner. What I allude to is cur want of common action in social affairs and our want of provision for (towers ahead. There are many rocks before us, above all secularism and infidelity, which are tearing the last shreds of dogma which Ang,licanism has preserved since leaving her ancient home—the true Church, and is now offering the nation as a sufficient system of belief. Where ' are our outposts, where is our camp, and all our prepara!ions , for defence and even attack when the battle comes? They 1 should be in the towns and villages of England, and should consist of chapels, schcols. and lecture rooms. Well, in a proenerous comity like this you many find it difficult to realise the utter absence of all these advantages elsewhere. In the large county of Northampton there are only four places which have resident priests, so that in many of its towns and almost every one of its villages Catholicism is unknown. The whole of Huntingd mshire contains one soli- tary priest. Bedfordshire has lint two, Buckinghamshire seven, and so on. though with a litte better average, through a dreary list of English and Welsh counties. Yet any- where where a permanent Sunday mass was established a congregation would spring up. TheWeslevans have planted little brick and mortar centres in half the villages in England, if would be well if we could imitate them. There is a little decreasing town in Leicestershire called Lutterworth, it may be called the cradle of the Reformation, for Wycklif lived there long ego in the 14th century. Well, latterly a priest went there to reside and establish the regular Sunday mass. The only Catholic in tie place was one old woman; at first there was no one found to serve mass, but before many Sundays passed, a boy who had been baptized a Catholic was reclaimed to the faith and performed this duty. The several families who had been Catholics or born so, added them- selves to the congregation. Then there was a convert. In short, after the space of 13 months since the priest's arrival, there is now a regular congregation of 25 persons. Can any rational person suppose that a similar Success would not attend a mission in any other such town—there are hundreds —where the faith is as yet. unknown ? If I may venture to make the remark, it seems to me there is no surer and better means of converting our country than helping to set "up small county missions, dotting them here and there like little paradises in the desert places of unbelief. A person who has been the means of bringing about a happy marriage and, to whom after many years those that have loF;en united bear a common debt of gratitude and good feeling as the pa th cause of their happiness, such a person may well be satisfied with his work of counsel. ACCIDENT AT HUTTON STATION:A signalman named Robert Gibson, employed on the London and Nolo - Western Railway, at lluyton Station, met with an accident, on Saturday morning last. Gibson, with others, was engag, d in unloading a waggon in a siding, when, by some means or other, a cask of white lead slipped and fell edge-ways on to one of his hands, inflicting serious injuries, lie was taken ti Dr. Packer, of Huyton,who dressed the wounds. Gib:ion is off duty, but his band is progressing as favourably as can be expected.

kept her without food. She was obliged to leave him; and as there was no law requiring a married woman to work in . .

order to relieve the husband of his responsibilities, and as her father and mother were not called upon to maintain her, application WAB made to Mr. Stuart, the relieving Milner, who investigated the case, and the parties went before the Guardians, who came to the conclusion that defendant

should pay 10s. a week. Defendant, who was present at the workhouse, said be would never have her back as long as be lived, and subsequently said to the relieving officer that he did not intend to pay the money. Defendant did not give his wife sufficient money to keep her, although he had always plenty of money and could go away on costly excursions. He was never short of money for his own purposes and in- dulgencies. He had been in receipt of £2 a week allowed to him for the maintenance of his child. He himself had stated that he had £1,300 somewhere, and he had stated that . .

, although he had given a bill over the tobacconists shop and stock, when the latter was sold the money was put in the bank for him.—Charles Maurice Stuart, relieving officer, said he was present when the application for relief was in- vestigated by the Guardians. He heard defendant say that he "would never have her back as long as he puffed." On . .

speaking to him subsequently defendant told him to "take , Out a summons; he should never pay the money, as his brothers advised him not to do so."—Cross-examined: Wit- ness did not see any signs of destitution about the applicant when she made the application. He found her living with , her parents in Chapel-street.—lsabella Harris said her father had at times maintained her when her husband failed to do so. Her husband never worked, and he treated her very badly. She had had a great many black eyes, and his violence towards her was very common. He stayed out all night many times, and four or five nights at a time. On one occasion he brought a man to live in the house, but she did not know why he did this unless it was to ruin her character. She did not like the man. The value of the stock in the shop was £750. In July last he went for a fortnight's holiday, and she heard from him from Cork. That excursion cost him £.37. She had to pay for his lug- gage when he came back.—Cross-examined: She never used violence to her husband before he used violence to her. She did use violence to him on one occasion, but she did not splinter his jaw nor produce the swelling on it. The swelling came through drink. She remembered hitting him on the cheek with the child's hoop after he had complained of what she reported to be the day's "takings." He went out soon after. After that she went to the Red Lion with Susan Naylor to look for him, but she did not stay there until eleven. It was twenty minutes past eleven whea she got borne, and not one o'clock.—Mr. Swift submitted that this was no justification, as a man married a woman for better or for worse, and if she turned out a dissolute woman—though be did not admit Mrs. Harris had so turned out—that was no ground for refusing to maintain her.—Mr. Riley said he was going to show that if there were any violence it was on the part of the wife, and that she departed voluntarily, and that her husband kept his house open for three months awaiting her return, but she never came back. The husband was not bound to maintain his wife" until she bad offered to return.—ln continued cross- examination, Mrs. Harris said she never pushed her hus- band in the street so violently that he fell. He was so drunk that he could not walk. She was not aware that she ever did commence drinking, but he had been a thoroughly drunken, dissolute man from the moment of their marriage. He was a good husband when sober, but violent when in drink. Charley Rigby was not brought in as Mr. Harris's protector because she had threatened to cut her husband's throat when asleep. She never threatened to do any such thing. He had broken several blood vessels.—Mr. Swift: If the blond vessels were broken, I suppose it was not with the work he did? No. (Laughter.)—Ann Wilson, of Liver- pool, and Sarah Rigby, domestic servant with the defend Int, gave evidence in support of the case; and Robert Deacon, tobacconist, Liverpool-road, said the defendant m trriel his daughter, and he was very sorry now that he did.—Cross- examined : He had found the money to employ Mr. Swift in this case.—Mr. Riley; And I believe you are prepared to find a great deal more money to ruin John ? Ruin him! No, you know better Mr. Riley; I don't make those remarks. Witness said that defendant told him that his brothers had made an arrangement through the Court of Chancery, and he was to receive £2,000, £7OO of which was to set him up in business as a tobacconist; the re- nsainder was to go for the child.—Mr. Riley, for the defence, said it was worth while to remind themselves that this public exposure in defendant's own town was not the only means which might have been taken on behalf of Mrs. Harris, to decide whether she was really justified in remain- ing away from her husband. She might have applied to a superior court for restitution of conjugal rights. She might have pledged her husband's credit for necessaries, and then it might have been ascertained by calm investigation whether he deserted her, or whether she departed from him with just cause.—Mr. Swift said if there were ten thousand other remedies it would not alter this.—The defendant was called, and stated that he never used violence to his wife, hut she had used violence to him. She bad thrown jugs and dishes at him, and he bore a mark beneath his eye canard by the child's hoop. He also bore marks of blows with a poker. He was not fit for manual labour, and twelve months ago broke a blood vessel. He did not get £2 a week now hut only a trifle now and then from his brothers, and the interest on the £l,3oo.—Mr. Swift cross-examined de- fendant, but not gaining'satisfactory answers, he asked defendant if he was drunk, to which defendant replied, "No: are you?" Mr. Swift sat down saying, "Well, he's a fool if he's nothing else."—The Bench made an order for 10s. a week.

VIOLENT CHARACTERS.—CharIes Chubb and John Chubb (brothers) were charged with assaulting Margaret Grimes on the 17th instant.—Prisoners pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Swift said he appeared on the part of the complainant, who made application the previous morning to Mr. William l'ilkington, who was the sitting magistrate, and he granted warrants against the prisoners. They were now brought up under those warrants. The case required two magistrates to hear and determine it; and he therefore asked for a remand.- -P.C. 72 said he knew the house, at Pm-r, where ' Mrs. Grimes lived, and on Monday evening he saw the complainant and the two prisoners in the house. They both struck her. Charles struck her more than once.—Prisoners were remanded until Monday, and they applied for bail.—Mr. Swift said he could only say the attack was part of a preconcertecl scheme, and one of them had threatened the woman in the town before they get to Parr where they lived. It was for his worship to judge whether they ought to he-admitted to bail or not, and no doubt Mr. Johnston would assist him in coming to a decision.—Superintendent Johnston said the prisoners were most violent characters. After a case on Monday they threatened Sergeant Banks, and that sergeant was hardly slfe. The question was this: Is this woman safe? Ile hardly thought so, and he should be far from saving so if he thought different. Mr. Swift said complainant had given one of the men notice to quit. but he would not go; and on Monday they went to the iIOURO for the parpese of carrying away Mrs. Grimes's things, and threatened to leave the country after they had done all the damage they could—The prisoner Charles said the brief that Mr. Swift held in his hands contained nothing but lies.—The prisoners were ordered to be bound themselves in £5O each, and two sureties of £2s.—Sureties were not forth- coming.

21ST L.R.V. SHOOTING, (ST. HEL-ENS). 15TH L.R.V. (L'POOL) V. 21sv L.R.V. (ST. HELENS). The above match took place at Altcar, on Saturday, the 14th inst. Weather wet ; light very dull, some of the targets at 600 ya,cls being almost invisible: wind slight. The St. Helens men won by 84 points. Private J. J. Tickle won the "Twenty-shilling Cup" for best score on winning side, with 8D points, making seven bulls at 500 yards. The visitors were most kindly entertained after the match at the Hightown Hotel, by the officers and members of the 15th.

ACTION FOR A SEAMAN'S WAGES —William Roberts, cap- tain of the Galloway Lass, brigantine, was summoned by Richard Sutton, seaman, for neglecting to nay the sum of £2, beimg the amount of wages due to him.—Mr. Burton appeared for the complainant. and said the vessel was a coasting one, and the articles were understood to be those usually employed. He, however, saw from an examination of them that there was a clause put at the end of the article, which read "and finally to be discharged at Port Madoc, or the Menai straits, at master's option." This was a very unusual clause ; and, in addition to this, the complainant would swear that on signing the articles they were not read over to him, nor was there a witness present as required by the Act. This conduct involved an offence by which the defendant had rendered himself liable to a fine of £s.—Com- plainant Wes called, and said he joined the vessel on the 14th March, at Garston. He signed the articles at sea, and no ' one was present at the time but the captain. They arrived at Runcorn on Thursday, and after helping to unload. he asked defendant for some money, but he refused to give him any. Defendant said he could go, but be should not pay him anything. On the Saturday afternoon, he told fhe captain that if he did not give him his money he would have to summons him, on which he replied he I might do as he liked—he did not care for the magistrates. The wages were at the rate of £2 ss. per month, and the the balance owing was £2 9s.—Samuel Jackson, a seaman, gave corroborative evidence.—Mr. Lake appeared for the dee fence, and said this was a much more important affair than a mere claim for wages. It was, in fact, one as to whether a man who had signed articles for six months, at a certain rate of wages, was entitled whenever he got to any port during that period, to discharge himself at his own sweet will, and so subject the captain to great inconvenience. The articles stated that the complainant agreed to serve from the 14th March to the 30tb of June, The ports of discharge were clearly shown, and until complainant had got to one of them the engagement between him and the captain could not be terminated. Defendant had bad a good deal of ' trouble owing to men leaving him in this manner, and' this was the reason that the port of discharge was men- , tioned. They had merely the ipse dixet of Mr. Burton as to the clause being an unusual one.—The defendant was called, and said that he, his wife, and the mate were present at the time the articles were signed. lie could not leave a port—owing to not being given his clearance note—unless he could show that the articles had been signed.—ln cross- examination, witness admitted that the irticles, as a whole, had been written out by a shipbroker. and he (witness) had added the clause about the two ports of discharge.—The wife of the defendant also gave evidence in support of the statement made by him.—The magistrates said they were of opinion that complainant was not entitled to his wages. owing to his not having performed his agreement, according to the articles, and the summons would be dismissed.

WINSFORD. WEILETAN CHAPEL, HILL Tor, WINSVORD.—On Sun- day afternoon and evening, two sermons were preached in i this chapel, in aid of the Sunday school funds, by the Rev. A. Roebucli, of Northwich. On each occasion there were large congregations. The choir rendered two anthems, "Let hills and lofty mountains," and "Exalt him all ye people," and the children sang suitable hymns accompanied by Miss A. Newell. The collections amounted to £l7 es. UNITED FREE METHODIST CHURCH, HIGH-STREET, WINSFORD.—In order to wipe off the existing debt and free the circuit, a sermon, followed by a circuit tea and lecture in the evening, was given on Monday last. The preacher and lecturer was the Rev. J. Kirsop, of Manchester, who delivered a very eloquent sermon in the afternoon. The congregation was not large, and the tea meeting was not so well attended as usual, partly through the non-publicity given to it, hut the leeture was well attended. Mr. Joseph Slater of Woodford Hall, presided. Mr. Kirsep, in com- mencing his lecture on "The World as it is and as it shall I be," remarked that all looked at the world from an interested point of view, and something like the Cornishman's prayer —"God bless me and my wife—God bless our John and his wife; and God bless us four and no more." He proposed to treat the lecture under two heads—lst, The world asit is; 2nd, As it shall be. It was a dark picture to look at the world as it is. Laws were broken, and "truth" often violated. Then again, how rife perjury was in our law courts. Honesty should be regarded as every one had a right to his brains and his bands. but robbery, fraud, and embezzlement, as well as deception, prevailed in everything. Adulteration, chicanery, &c., prevailed on every side, awl people forgetful 01 the golden rule, Whatsoever ye would that men should do unto you do ye also unto them." Purity was often violated; and in Christian England our divorce courts and evil legislation might make us cry with the leper, "Un- clean! unclean !" Intemperance was our national vice, and comprehended all the sins in the deealogue, while many looked upon nothing so worthless as human life. Religion might be Jivided into three classes. First, few would now , call themselves Atheists; they are non-Theists, Agnostics, &c. Second, those who professed true religion With regard to our social state, war was still waged, and the parties who had caused the quarrel took no part in it, but left it to men who had no animus against each other, and homes were rendered desolate to gratify the ambition of a few. Slavery was another blot en the world as it is. Caste hindered the gospel in many countries, but the march of education was causing many improvements, and they had not to draw on imagination to depict the "world as it will be." They had only to turn to prophecy. All evil should be abolished, nation should not rise against nation, slavery would be a thing of the past, all false forms of religions, and all intemperance would come to an end, while Holiness I would become a part of life. The universal motto should be. "As for me and my house we will serve the Lord." Civil government and family government would still exist. There would be national legislation, but soldiers would be abolished there would be social distinction, but the poor would be no longer snubbed by his richer brother. People would not be taught by miracles, but teachers and preachers would still be wanted. Denominational disturbances would be wiped away, hut some distinctions would always exist. Education, arts, science, &c. would all aid the Gospel in bringing about this state Of things. The press, ateam, and telegraph were great powers, and were helping forward the time when men should see the cross upheld, and adore Him who died on it. The usual votes of thanks and the Doxology concluded the evening. The choir sang an anthem and several hymns, Miss Buckley presiding at the

MR. PERCY DAVIES AND THE BENCH: A SCHNII —Wm. Dutton, a young man, was charged with using abusive lan- guage calculated to provoke a breach of the peace to Alice I Atherton, on the 2ad inst.—Dutton had issued a cross i summons against Mrs. Atherton.—Mr. Harrison appeared ' for Mrs. Atherton, and Mr. Percy Davies for Dutton.—Mr. I Harrison said the parties lived at Sankey Bridges, and were 1 near neighbours. On the date named whilst Mrs. Atherton I was in her yard talking to a young woman, Dutton came , up to her and made use of the filtliar language complained of.—At this point Mr. Davies requested that all the wit- nesses should leave the court.---I.n answer to Mr. Davies, Mrs. Atherton said she had been Dutton's mother-in-law, but his wife died about twelve months ago and he had married another woman.—A witness called to support the charge was being cross-examined by Mr. Davies, when a conversation took place between Mr. Davies and the Bench. At in conclusion Mr. Artingstall told the witness to "stand down."—Mr. Davies: I have not finished my cross-examina- tion yet.—Mr. Artingstall : You have cross-examined her enough. (To witness) Stand down.—Mr. Davies: I must protest against such gross injustice. It is most abominable in a court of law. You are put here by the public to do a duty, and when you sit there you ought to do your duty to 1 the public. You have no right to do anything like this to my I client lam not allowed to conduct my case, and you make a I point of it every time I come here.—Mr. Harrison: I cer- tainly thought you had concluded-your cross-examination. —Mr. Artinktstall: He had.—Mr. Davies: I have not com- pleted my cross-exatnination. You would not give me leave to ask her questions.—Mr. Artingstall : You asked her quite sufficient.—Mr. Davies: I protest against the case going on further. I apply for an adjournment, and I hope the Bench will take notice of what I say.--Mr. Artingstall : Oh, yes. We alkali take notice of what you say.—Mr. Davies: I didn't come here to be insulted by a magistrate.— Mr. Artingstall : I have not insulted you.—Mr. Davies: You are older than I am, and certainly old enough to know a great deal better.—Mr. Harrison: I thought you had done, certainly.—Mr. Davies: How could I—Mr. Artingstall: I hope the reporters will take notice of this langnage.—Mr. Davies: And I hope the reporters will take notice that you refuse to let me conduct my cross-examination. I should I like to take the ruling ot the Bench upon it.—Several wit- ' nesses were then examined as to the languasre used by defendant, and Mr. Davies addressed the Bench for the de- fence. His client had worked for Messrs. Clare and Ridgway for 'a. great number of years, and had had the best of characters. He was incapable of using the language I ascribed to him. He (Mr. Davies) was convinced that the evidence of complainant and her witnesses was a "pack of lies" from beginning to end.—Mr. Artingstall said there was nothing said as to the respectability of the defendant. The complainant herself had said he was a respectable man, and that Was stronger than anything he (Mr. D.vies) could say.—Mr. Harrison: Much stronger.—Mr. Davies said he much doubted that. He had a case against the woman, but he was in a very awkward position, because he could not prove his case in the absence of his witness, and he applied for an adjournment.—Mr. Arting,stall : You have got three • witnesses here.—After some further conversation, the case proceeded.—Mr. Davies called three witnesses, whose evidence was directly oppovd to that of complainant and her witnesses.—The Bench retired to consider their decision, and on returning Mr. Artingstall said they considered the ease a most disreputable one on both sides. There were six of one and half a dozen of the 'other. Defendant and com- plainant were each bound over in their own recognisances to keen the peace for six months.

SEQUEL TO A CABMEN'S STRIKE AT WARRINGTON. At the Borougk Police Court, on Tuesday, before Major Cartwright, Alderman Webster, and Councillor Fairclough Arthur Milwood, Fred Westhead, John Perdue, James Jordan, and James Davies were charged, under warrant, with having, on Monday, for the purpose of compelling Thomas Longshaw to abstain from working for the Lion Hotel Company, Limited, unlawfully, vrrongfully, and without legal authority intimidated him. Milwood, Pend" and Jordan pleaded guilty, and the others not guilty. The Chief-Constable (Mr. Hunt) said the defendants were cab drivers at the Lion Hotel, as was also the prosecutor. On the previous morning Mr. Burns, foreman of the yard, gave orders to the men to whitewash certain stables, and first one and then another refused to do the work. At that time prosecutor was out with a'bus at the railway station, and, having brought a traveller to the hotel was going out again, when he was told by the prisoners that they had struck work and he must do the same. He, however, went out with the 'bus, but when in Bridge-street, near Mr. Pick- mere's stores, he was stopped by the prisoners, who took the horse out of the conveyance, leaving the vehicle in the street and allowing the horse to find its way back as best it I could. The horse returned to the hotel, and sometimeaf ter- wards the harness was found on the stable floor. The pro- secutor again harnessed the horse to the conveyance and went down to Bank Quay station, where he was followed by the prisoners, one or two of whom seized hold of him by the collar and used serious threats to him. The Town Clerk should have been present to prosecute, but as he had not arrived the directcrs wished for the case lobe adjourned. Re (Mr. Hunt) thought the evidence would be sufficiently fell to alio% the Bench to deal with the men. Mr. Burns, the foreman at the Lion Hotel, gave evidence confirmatory of Mr. Hunt's statement. He said it had bee* understood that the men were to whitewash the stables in turns; but one man having refused to do so, they all said they would go out fiist. Witness said, " You can take your own course," and they at once fetched their whips and walked away. The Prosecutor, speaking as to the stoppage of the 'bus in Bridge-street, stated that Perdue got hold of the horse's head, and Westhead jumped on the seat and uncoupled the reins. Westhead, Perdue, and Jordan took the horse out of the carriage. He did notice Milwood there. Milwood said he was out with a cab until half-past eight. In answer to Major Cartwright, he saia he pleaded ,guilty to helping to pull the horse out of the 'bus. The other pri- soners expressed sorrow for what they had done. Major Cartwright remarked that it seas a conspiracy to stop the whole of the cab business of the establishment, and because the man Longshaw would not join them in an un- just act the prisoners set upon him, and said," Well, if you won't come out we will force you." They had an t.pportu- nity given them of going quietly away, but they took the law into their own hands and interfered with their employers' property. Such like work could not be tolerated. People must be allowed to conduct without interruption. After conferring with his brother magistrates, Major Cart- wright said the prisoners richly deserved to be sent to prison, betas it was seldom they had a case of this nature before them the Bench were inclined to deal very leniently with them. He hoped it would be a lesson to them. [Prisoners: It will] Milwood, Westhead, Perdue, And Jordan would be fined 30A., including costs, or in default a month's impri- nment. Davies, who did not appear to have taken so great a part in the matter, would be fined 208., including costs, or in 13efau1t 14 days.

THE EXA.MINER, SATURDAY MAY 21, 1881. I CIIESFIIRE SALT DISTRICTS COM- PENSATION BILL. The Select Committee of the 'House of Commons ap- pointed to consider th;s bill sat on Monday for the eighth time, under the presidency of Sir Sidney Waterlow, when further evidence was given on behalf of the salt proprietors opposing the bill. Mr. C. E. De Rance. I G.S., in re-examination by Mr. Balfour Brown, denied th .nputation that, if the promoters bad paid his fees, he awn, we given evidence in favour of the bill, had his conclusio, after an inspection of the dis- trict not been in accordance with those of the promoters. Before he visited the salt district of Cheshire he was under the erroneous impression that the brine used by the manu- facturers was an artificial product, but he found that he was totally misinformed. There was historical evidence that subsidences bad taken place long before the pumping of brine commenced. Mr. Maskelyne : The evidence of the witness is very im- portant, and it seems to me that if the points are established the promoters of the bill will have some difficulty in proving the preamble. Mr. Baldwin Latham, F.G.S., civil engineer, stated that he had great experience in hydraulic engineering, and was well acquainted with the geographical character of Cheshire, particularly of Nantwich, of which town he was a native. There had been great difficulty in obtaining fresh water from underground, not only in Cheshire, but in Warwick- shire, and other districts where there were similar strata, in consequence of the brine miied with water. He had found wells at Nantwicb containing 16 to 20 grains of salt to the gallon, and had known a brine spring to issue into the river Weaver at a point known as Welsh Row Bridge. The aa erage quality of brine below the town was 12 grains of salt to the gallon, and at higher levels outside the town about 5 grains to the gallon. He knew the nacres or lakes of Cheshire, and he believed that they were caused by the dis- solving out of beds of salt below. He had no doubt that brine was produced by the rainfall entering into the beds of rock salt at the outcrop, and that underground water was I entirely dependent on the fall of rain. The brine springs he had spoken of were subject to reasonable fluctuations. and that proved conclusively to his mind that the water taken in at the outcrop dissolved the salt, and emptied itself in the river. He did not think that pumping would increase the dissolving out of the salt, as the moment the limit of pumping was reached the springs would diminish in exact ratio to the amount of pumping, and, if the pumping was exhaustive, cease to flow. The pumping of brine only dried the natural springs, which would otherwise have found their way into the Weaver. The subsidences were due to the same cause—the percolation of rain through the surface of the ground forcing the brine out. By Mr. Wright: There could be no flow or brine unless there were channels for it to flow in. If the pumping ceased, the river Weaver would become much more saline than it was at present. He estimated that 75,000 tons of salt were now annually carried away by the Weaver by natural means. Mr. Charles M. Blades stated that he had been an analy- tical chemist at Northwich for the past ten years. He had made various analyses of the rivers Weaver, Dane, and Croco. He found that the first-named at Middlewich con- tained 3.5 grains of salt per gallon, the Croco 936 grains, and the two united 4.68 grains. These samples were taken on the 21st March last, a time of the year when the rivers were swollen with floods. The Dane at Sbipbrookbridge, near Northwich, he found to contain 14 04 grains per gal- lon, and at Leftwich 2457 grains. The river Weaver above the top flash of water contained 9.36 grains of chloride of sodium, and in the top flash 8.19 grains. Between Hartford and a point known as Barrow Locks, near Northwich, he found that the water of the Weaver contained 140.4 grains of salt per annum, but that was exceptional, and would be accounted for by salt thrown overboard from vessels being loaded. The Weaver at Town-bridge, Northwich, contained 81.90 grains of salt. He had examined brine springs at Nantwich, and found 36 ounces and 35 grains of salt to each gallon. Witness had known the neighbourhood of North- wich for eleven years. He lived close to the banks of the river. His house had subsided considerably, but he attri- buted this to the dredging of the river. Mr. l'ember said he would now have read extracts from books in the British Museum, giving historic evidence as to the state of the country near the salt mines long before human memory. The Chairman said he should certainly allow the other side to put in extracts to balance those read by Mr. Pember. Mr. Falk, of Winsford, deposed that he had made re- searches into the history of the Cheshire salt trade, and traced subsidences in reference to the natural flow of brine as far back as the 16th century. The extracts showed that the salt had liquified close to the banks of the river, and rendered houses uninhabitable by. subsidence in 1819. In 1713 the ground near Weaver Hall, Winsford, suddenly fell in, leaving a bole 9 yards in diameter, and the cavity filling with salt water. Mr. H. E. Falk, salt proprietor, Winsford, and president of the Cheshire Salt Chamber of Commerce,said he believed there was an underground flow of water to Winsford from the high elevation of Delarnere Forest, and that this, and not the pumping, was the cause of subsidences. He agreed with the geological evidence even. The committee then adjourned. On Tuesday Mr. Hermann Eugene Falk, salt mine pro- prietor, Winsford, resumed his examination, stating that the flashes at Winsford were not due to the pumping of the brine at Winsford. If there was no pumping of the brine, it would be carried to the river Weaver, or in some other direction. He had a mine ten acres in extent, and he had not a foot of brine in a day, although two shafts which worked it were only one hundred and fifty yards distant from a spring, out of which he pumped about 120,000 tons of white salt a year. Were the brine to come on the sur- face of the land the latter would become waste, as was the case at Newchurch Common, Glover's Moss, and Oakmere. There was neither an inlet nor outlet in Oakinere, notwith- standing which fact, the water was 8 feet lower in the evening than in the morning. If the brine was not inter- Opted it would come out in the springs. He was of opinion that if pumping were to cease in the valley of the Weaver, if the climate was very dry, the valley of the Mersey would become one vast run of hutch filled with rock salt. Brine springs were to be found everywhere in Cheshire, especially in the valley of the Weaver. The springs of Northwich were saturated with 15 per cent of salt. There was evidence to show that there had been considerable subsidences in olden times, and that there was a long time ago a large number of brine springs. There had been little or no im- provement in the art of salt manufacture since the days of the Romans and possibly since the times of the Druids. About 1,00400 tons of salt were manufactured annually at Winsford, 500,000 at Northwich, and 100,000 tons at Sand- bach. A tax upon salt had always been resisted since feudal times, and he was of opinion that if one were im- posed the salt trade would virtually be consigned to its grave. About one-third of the whole of the salt exported was shipped at Liverpool. Amongst other effects of the salt trade had been the creation of the alkali trade, at St. Helens, Whines, and Runcorn, between 300,000 and 400,000 tons of salt being wee' in the manufacture. It had also attracted the cotton printing and bleaching trades to Man- chester.

WARRINGTON BO kRD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the Board was held, on Wed- nesday, at the Workhouse. Mr. J. Harrison occupied the chair, and there were also present:—Revs. J. Tongs, G. F Roberts. and B. B. Prescott; Messrs. Greening, Woolfall, Mackie, Heaton, Derbyshire, Houghton, Winstanley, Fair- hurst, Hunt, Woods, Blackhurst, Cartwright, Gibson, and .1 C. Sutton (clerk). RE-APPOINTMENT OF A MEDICAL OFFICER. Mr. N 1 INSTANLET moved that the appointment of Dr. Joseph, as medical officer of No. 1 district, for three years, be confirmed. Mr. DARE/SHIRE seconded the motion, which was carrieil. THE NEW SCHOOLS. Messrs. Pierpoint and Son, architects, recommended that the sum of £350 be loaid to Mr. George Napier, on account of work done at the homes and schools. The CHAIRMAN: These come with great rapidity upon US. Mr. 'WiNsrasmuy : The greater rapidity the better, be- cause it shows the work is done. The CHAIRMAN: Well, of course, if the work is pro- gressing. Mr. WINSTANLEY: I may inform the Board that on Friday last the committee met at Pedgete and inspected the new schools, and the progress and character of the work appeared quite satisfactory. The rcommendation was confirmed. THE ANNUAL TRIP. Mr. WOOLFALL asked if the Board would sanction the children having a trip. There was little doubt that mem- bers of the Board and gentlemen outside would be glad to undertake the management of the trip. No money was asked from the Board, and it was a great treat for the children. The CHAIRMAN: Is it not rather early? Mr. WOOLFILL : There are many preliminaries. The trip may not take place until July. It was decided, on the proposition of Mr. DARBYSHIRE, seconded by Mr. HEATON. that the children have their annual trip; and a committee was subsequently appointed to make the necessary arrangements. THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL CHARGES. Mr. DARBYSHIRE called attention to an account from the Infectious Diseases Hospital, in which they charged 14s. per day. £3 or £4 was charged for three days, which showed, he thought, that the Board should get their own contagious hospital as soonas possible, because they were being charged a very large amount in this case. The CLERK: That woman was only in two days, I think. What is the bill? Mr. HARETSHIRE : The whole bill is £9 ss. Bd. The CLERK: From the 2nd to the'slh of February. But there is a lot of destroyed clothing, and all that. Mr. HAREYSIIIRE said it appeared because the Guardians had no arrangement with the Warrington Sanitary Authority they could charge anything. The CHAIRMAN: Bat! think they only charge us accord- ing to a certain scale they have laid down. Mr. DARBYSTIIRE : It appears to be a very high scale. The CHAIRMAN: It does, indeed. Mr. COOPER reminded the Guardians that the Rural Sanitary Authority were paying £l3O a year independent of the Guardians. The Rev. J. YONGE explained that the largest items in the bill appeared to be for hospital bedding burned by order of the ospital superintendent. The bill was not strictly for hospital charges. The CHAIRMAN: Oh, no; I thought it was impossible to be. But still, two guineas is a large sum. Mr. WINSTANLEY thought the Clerk ought to impress upon the Guardians the necessity of getting their hospital ready. They were paying that day £4O for what would have coat them £5 if the Board had bad their hospital ready. Mr. DARBYSHIRE: But these charges I contend ought to be borne by the Urban Sanitary Authority. Major CARTWRIGHT : I thought the question of charges in regard to the Infectious Diseases Hospital had been settled. The CHAIRMAN: No; we have no arrangement. Major CARTWRIGHT: Is that Newton case settled? The CHAIRMAN: Don't the Commissioners intend to pay the bill? Mr. WINSTANLEy: I think not. Major CARTWRIGHT : Then they won't adept your sug- gestion to pay one half? Mr. WINSTANLEY: No; I think not. Major CARTWRIGHT : Well, I think they ought to be made to pay. The Crum:vex: Yes, but unfortunately we cannot make them. Major CARTWRIGHT : Are you sure? The CHAIRMAN: Yes. I only wish we could, because it is a very shabby proceeding. Mr. DARBYSHIRE said it was on account of the Newton Commissioners not being an organised body to take charge of infectious cases that the Board could not make them pay. They were so now, and he did not think such a case would occur again. The CHAIRMAN : You see the Newton Commissioners never made any contract with the Corporation. It was done by our servants, and whether rightly or wrongly I will not say, but I am sure Mr. Mackey did what he thought best. Major CARTWRIGHT : Mr. Mackey had nothing to do with it. The CHAIRMAN: They were sent here in the first instance, and Mr. Mackey, if I am rightly informed, as soon as he discovered that they were affected by disease, sent them to the hospital. Major CARTWRIGHT : The doctor did. The CHAIRMAN: By whose orders were they sent there ? The MASTER: The doctor's. Major CARTWRIGHT : Well, if we have no power, we can't recover. The CHAIRMAN: No, we cannot. Mr. WINSTANLEY said the law clerk to the Newton Com- missioners advised them that they had no power to pay the account. If they did so they would certainly be sur- charged.

THE GAS BILL. Major CARTWRIGHT drew attention to a gas bill amount- ing to £57, and asked if it was not unusually large. The CLERIC did not know. The MASTER said it was considerably higher than when the Board were making gas—in fact, it was more than double. Mr. WOODS Must say that when the Board were making their own gas they could not see. It was no use talking about making gas they could not see by. CouRFsPoNDENCE. Letters were read from the Local Government Board assenting to the remuneration of Mr. McClelland, vaccina- tion officer for Warrington, as increased; and approving of the Board meeting fortnightly instead of weekly. • HARD-WORKED OFFICIAL ASKS FOR AN INCRAASK OF SALARY. The CHAIRMAN read the following letter : " Warrington, May 18, 1881 —Gentlemen,—ln justice to myself I feel compelled to ask for an Increase of salary. As you are aware there are a great many casuals come to the souse for shelter. There were 22,909 during the last two years, and my duty begins at 6 a.m. in looking after the task of work which the casuals have to perform, and to see that they perform it before leaving. In the evening the casuals came at all times from 6 p.m. to 12, and even on to 1 o'clock a.m., making a day's work 18 hours, or approaching to it, every day. In most places where the casuals are admitted up to midnight, or after, there 14 a night porter to take the duty after a certain hour at night. Hoping for your favourable con- sidereion, lam, .k?., JAMES CURRY.' Notice of motion was given that the application be con- sidered at the next meeting.

GROUNDLESS ALLEGATIONS AGAINST THE MANAGEMENT. The following letter was read : • " Regent-street, Golborne,street, Warrington, May 9th, 1881.—To the Chairman of the Board of Guardians.—Sir,—l wish respectfully to call your attention to a practice which 'seems to prevail with respect to the paupers who are resident in the Workhouse. I understand that on those days when they are permitted to go out of the House for the purpose of visiting their friends, they are not allowed to go out in the clothes which they usually wear in the House, but they are obliged to put on the clothes which they had on when they came to the house. There would not be anything to complain about in this custom if the clothes wore kept in • proper condi. tion. But it seems they are not so kept. They are taken from the poor unfortunate people who are compelled to seek the shelter of the Workhouse, and their old clothes, which are often filthy enough at the time, are thrown together in a heap, and there lie a disgusting heap of fi'thy old rags; and when the day comes round that the paupers are allowed to visit their ac- quaintances or friends, the clothes which they usually wear are taken from them, and their old clothes are given them to put on, although they are, from the manner in which they are kept in a most abominably disgraceful con- dition. I had a visit last Tuesday from one of the aged female paupers, and the stench from the dress which she had upon her was of the most horrid kind.. There were two customers in my shop at the time who can testify to the truth of what, I have here written. The wearer of the dress said she had not had it on for many months previous. Such filth was enough to breed a pestilence. I have taken this bberty of calling your attention to above, as I have no doubt you will take the proper means to abate such a vile and danger- ous nuisance. Indeed the effect produced upon me from the unpleasant smell of her clothing has been so seve,e that I have not been wel since.—Yours resp:ctlully, MIRY LONGSHAW." Rev. J. YONG& asked whether as a matter of fact, the statement was correct. The CHAIRMAN very much doubted it, because he under- stood when poor persons came to the house their clothes were thoroughly cleansed and put by in good order. Major CARTWRIGHT thought this a very unwarrantable letter, and more especially coming from the person it did. He thought before she Lad written such a letter as that she should have been conversant with the house, and called at the house, or at all events, to have addressed that note to the Visiting Committee. The committee would have been glad to see Mrs. Longshaw, and to hear anything she had to say in the matter, without her writing • letter of that description. All the charges were totally untrue; that he did know. The CHAIRMAN: Well, I should think they were myself. Major CARTWRIGHT : The master of the House and the matron also will be able to tell you when inmates ask for a day to go out to visit their friends they always go in the Workhouse clothes. If they ask for their discharge they have their own clothing, unless they come before this Board and get a grant for something better. Their clothes are packed up and patio a room to be ready for them when they go out. I have no doubt in this case ii there is any truth in the statement 4 all, in regard to the clothing, it was the clothing bel nging to the person when she came into the House. She would ask for her discharge and get the cloth- ing. You see she mentions no names. When persons. are

prepared to write letters of that description they ought to be prepared with the name of the party who called upon them. We don't know anything as to who it is. I think it is a very irregular letter indeed, and a letter I certainly should not have expected from a person of Mrs. Longshaw's position. Mr. lirescanuissr thought the best course was not to dis- cuss the letter. It contained damaging charges against the management of the house, and the best plan was to refer the letter to the House Committee. Mr. A. MACKIE was about to suggest the same course. HE, did not know the writer, but presumed she was a respectable ratepayer. The CHAIRMAN: She is the wife of an ex-guardian. Mr. A. MACKIN said that being the case, she ought to know something of what she was writing. For the credit of the Guardians the statement contained in the letter should be enquired into It was a complaint which, if true, Mrs. Long- shaw had a perfect right to make, but which, if not true, she ought to be, and probably would be, quite as willing to withdraw it as to make it. Mr. GREENING had always understood that when paupers came into the house the first thing they did was to take the clothes from them, disinfect the clothes, and put them away. If that was so, it seemed strange that they should be in a filthy condition. (Hear, hear.) He could not understand how they could be. He understood that the regulations were such that no pauper was allowed to go out of the house in their own clothes without special permission. He thousen there must be some other explanation of the letter. The CHAIRMAN said it seemed incredible that clothes were in a filthy condition. Major CARTWRIGHT : What I complain of is the letter. Mr. A. MACKIE : If it is true there is nothing wrong. Major CARTWRIGHT: I think it is very wrong. Rev. J. YONCIE suggested that the Visiting Committee should at once make an investigation as to the way paupers clothes were treated, so that the charge could be exploded. After some conversation Mr. Yonge's suggestion was adopted. At the conclusion of the special business the committe made an investigation, and on returning to the Board room, Major CARTWRIGHT said they bad examined the several bundles of clothes and found no extraordinary smell upon them. When a person was admitted to that house his own clothing was taken and " stoved," as it was termed, with brimstone. The clothes were then packed up, and a label was placed upon them containing the name, date, and number of articles. They were then put into the stores, which were entirely disconnected from the house. The matron had nothing whatever to do with them, and he did not suppose the master had beyond taking care of them. There were only a few inmates allowed to go out in their own clothes so that they were at a loss to know who it was that had called upon Mrs. Longshaw. He thought every gentleman agreed with him that there was no smell, and unless they heard something to the contrary, they were of opinion that Mrs. Longshaw was mistaken in some way or that matters had been misrepresented to her, and she on the spur of the moment had written the letter. If Mrs. Long- shaw thought proper to come to the Visiting Committee meeting at any time they would hear any explanation she wished to make. and the committee would be able to satisfy her. At the same time he thought the letter ought not to have been written. The CHAIRMAN : It is the opinion that it was not justi- fied. Mr. A. MACKIE thought even more than that. He was sure some of them must be very gratified to find things in the very excellent way in which they were. The paupers and ratepayers might he assured that the clothes were kept, as far as they could judge, as carefully as if they were in a barracks or any other public institution. . Mr. GREENING thought it a great pity Mrs. Longshaw did not make more enquiry before she wrote such a defamatory letter, and that it was quite impossible there could be any smell about the clothes. The fact was the clothes were 10 times cleaner when they went out of the House than when they came in. Mr. DARBYSHIRE said the general arrangements in keep- ing the clothes in the condition in which they were ap- peared to him to be excellent. If the case was the one he believed it to be. he had made enquiry and found that the woman had been in the habit of going out of the House and returning with onions, red-herrings, bacon, matches, and several other things in her pockets. If it was the same person, and she had an accumulation of these things in her pockets after she left the House, there would be a bad smell Rev. J. Yoxou was gratified the matter had been enquired. into so promptly audio such a eatisfactorymanner, although he did not know whether they were justified in being so hard upon Mrs. Longshaw as Mr. Greening seemed to be. The CHAIRMAN remarked that it was very satisfactory to find such a concensus of opinion amongst the committee as to the condition of the institution and the groundlessness of the charges in the letter. He was astonished to read the letter, but he was glad to find it was a mare's nest. THIS SCHOOLS coatestrrem.—Tnn MASTER AND SCHOOL- MASTER COME TO TERMS. FRODSTIAM. CHM/CR MISSIONARY SERMONS AND MHRTING AT FROD- SHAM.—The annual sermons in aid of the Church Mission- ary Society were preached on Sunday, morning and evening, in the iron church, by the Rev. J. H. Acheson, of Chester. Both services were well attended. On Monday evening the annual meeting was held in the Town Hall, the Vicar, the Rev. H. B. Blom, pt.( siding. Short addresses were delivered by the Chairman, the Revs. W. G. Knocker, vicar of Alvanley, and J. W. Consterdine, of Alderley Edge. Col- Jections were made at the close of each service and the meeting in aid of the society's funds.

SUCCESSFUL LAW FIAMINATIOW.—We are glad to learn that Mr. Charles Rune Thomas, youngest son of the late Mr. Robert Thomas, solicitor of this town, has successfolly vassed the "Intermediate Examination" of the Incorporated Law Society of London. He is now articled with Air. Brewis, town clerk, and passed the preliminary law exami- ration 0/1 the 14th May, 18113.

RESCOT UNION.—TO BUILDERS.—The Guardians of this U,,ion are desirous of receiving TENDERS for the erection of a Chapel at the Workhouse, to accommodate 250 persons. Plans and specifications may be seen, and further , particulars obtained, at the Colon Offices, Whiston' after Tues- day next. Sealed Tenders endorsed "Chapel" to be sent to me not later than 10 o'clock in the morning, of the 2nd June nrxt, on which day they will be opened. The Guardians do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any Tender. B. H. HARTLEY. Union Clerk. Union Offices. 'A histon, Prescot, 19th May, 11381.

TO TAR DISTILLERS AND PYRITES ACID MANUFACTURERS. THE GAS COMMITTER of the ST. HELENS CORPORATION invite TENDERS for the surplus Tar produced at these works for one and two years respectively, commencing on the Ist July next. Quantity about 600 tons per annum. Also for the same period TENDERS for the supply of Pyrites Acid of a strength not less than 148 T 0/s; quantity about 150 tons per annum; to be delivered into these works in tanks, in such weekly quantities as may be specified in writing by the gas engineer. Sealed tenders, stating the net price per ton properly endorsed, and addressed to the Chairman of the Oa; Committee, to be delivered to the undersigned (from whom forms of tender may be obtained), not later than Tues Jay, the 24th inst. The committee do not bind themselves to accept the highest or any tender, for the tar, or the lowest or any tender for the pyrites acid.—By order, EDWARD DYSON, Secretary. Gas Office, St. Helens, 12th May, 1881.

TO STONE MERCHANTS AND OTHERS.—The RUNCORN IMPROVEMRNT COMMISSIONERS are prepared to receive TENDERS for about 500 tons of Stone suitable for road metal to be delivered at intervals as per instructions from time to time. The Tenders to state a price per ton del,vered at the following places in Runcorn, viz :—Stone Croft, Top Locks; Crane Wharf, Halton-road; and Stone Wharf, Old Quay. Each Tender to be accompanied with a sample of the I stone proposed to be supplied and to state a price for unbroken, and a price for hand broken into two-inch cubes. Tenders to be sent not later than Mon- day, the 30th day of May, 1881, addressed to the Chairman of the Highway and Sanitary Committee, Public Offices, Rurcorn, and endorsed "Tender for road metal." The Commissioners do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any tender.— By order, W. BROOKES. Secretary. Runcorn, May 12th, 1881.

MAKIN SON AND WILCOCK, in returning their sincere thanks to their numerous patrons and the public generally for the very kind and liberal support they have hitherto received. hope, by strict attention to the interests of their clients, and the prompt and faithful discharge of their duties, to continue to merit the same; the more so, as they are able to offer ad- vantages not generally enjoyed by those engaged in the same business, Mr. Makinson having had from early youth practieal experience of the English Timber, Stone and Building Trades, and of Farming in all its branches, being at the present time a farmer himselt on a large scale ; and, in addition, having served his apprenticeship to the ENGINEERING and MILLWRIGHT busi- ness, besides having had, during the last TEN years, consider- able practis2e in Valuing and Selling Colliery, Quarry, and other Machinery and Working Plant.
